Ask Maps is starting to find appointments online and call local businesses for customers. Here's what Business Profile says about Google's automated calls.

Open appointment slots at beauty, pet care, auto and home-repair businesses are starting to show up in Ask Maps, Google Maps’ AI chat. Google says Ask Maps can look for these appointments online and phone the businesses for a customer.

The feature is part of a set of Ask Maps updates that started rolling out Monday on Android and iOS. Appointment finding is launching first in the U.S.

Business Profile already has a setting for calls Google makes on behalf of customers. Google’s post doesn’t say whether Ask Maps calls follow it.

Google’s post describes appointment finding in Ask Maps this way:

“Now, with new agentic capabilities, you can choose to have Ask Maps find beauty, pet care, auto and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you.”

Google’s example request is “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps then shows openings at nearby businesses “so it’s easy to decide what to book,” according to the post.

Google’s demo shows Ask Maps confirming the service, location and preferred time before checking availability.

Google’s Business Profile help page on automated calls says that when customers use Google Search or Maps to connect with a business, Google might call that business on their behalf to complete the request. The requests it lists include booking appointments and confirming the price and availability of services. If a business works with online booking providers, the page says Google may book through the partner or call the business directly.

Verified businesses manage these calls in Business Profile under More, then Business Profile settings, then Advanced settings. The section labeled “Google automated calls and text messages” has a toggle for “Bookings and inquiries from customers.” A business can also ask a Google caller to stop calling.

The help page says these calls are available in every U.S. state except Indiana, Louisiana, Minnesota, Montana and Nebraska.

Google has called local businesses for searchers before. In July 2025, I covered the rollout of AI calling in Search, where people searching for a service such as auto repair or a pet groomer can tap “Have AI check pricing” and have Google call several providers nearby. Google’s help page for that feature says the person then gets an email with quotes.

When it launched in Search, a Google spokesperson said the AI picks which businesses to contact based on traditional local search rankings. Google’s Ask Maps post doesn’t say how Ask Maps chooses businesses to check or call.

At I/O in May, Google said people could ask it to call businesses “for select categories like home repair, beauty or pet care.” Three of the four Ask Maps categories match those examples.

Google’s Ask Maps post says the chat is starting to expand to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany and the U.K., bringing it to more than 200 countries and territories. Itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered, while appointment finding starts in the U.S.

Ask Maps puts openings from nearby businesses in front of a customer in the same conversation where they pick a place to book. For beauty, pet care, auto and home-repair businesses in the U.S., that’s a new place to win an appointment, and Ask Maps can call them to check openings.

The “Bookings and inquiries from customers” toggle in Business Profile is the control Google documents for calls it makes for customers through Search and Maps. Check where yours is set, and let whoever answers your phone know these calls come from Google on a customer’s behalf.

Google says more regions are coming soon for Ask Maps’ appointment finding, though the post names none and gives no date. Watch the Business Profile help page for word on whether the “Bookings and inquiries from customers” toggle and the five-state exclusion cover Ask Maps’ calls.

#7450. The Independent Journalism Atlas looks at “wells” and “springs” in news deserts

What do we mean when we talk about news deserts?

The term has become a shorthand for areas devoid of local news coverage. But a new essay from the Independent Journalism Atlas recalls that when Penny Abernathy popularized the term through her research, she used it to describe a more nuanced picture:

Things grow in a desert, she told Medill’s Tim Franklin in 2024, just not as abundantly. Asked why she didn’t say “news vacuum,” she answered, “There’s news; it’s just not necessarily the quality and the quantity of what you would find elsewhere.” RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026To show what information can look like in news deserts, the Independent Journalism Atlas — an initiative that aims to “[document] independent creators who inform, educate, and advance public knowledge outside traditional media structures,” cofounded by Liz Kelly Nelson, Justin Bank, and 2025 Nieman Fellow Ryan Kellett — took a closer look at 46 of the 238 news desert counties identified in this year’s State of Local News report from Medill. RELATED ARTICLEMany people who live in “local news deserts” don’t feel deprived of local news, study findsLaura Hazard OwenFebruary 10, 2026“Look at the ground and news moves like water,” writes Bank. “It doesn’t stop at a county line. It runs off the surface, sinks underground and comes up wherever someone digs.” The team found that “in more places than the desert map shows, someone has picked up a shovel.” (That might help explain why people who live in news deserts don’t feel deprived of local news.) The team identifies a few patterns in how information looks and travels in news deserts, including “surface” information, wells, and springs. Posts from the local sheriff, weather alerts, and obituaries from the funeral home are all examples of “surface” information that “runs off,” Bank writes, typically telling you what happened without telling you why. Wells are newsrooms that form when a local paper shutters. The team points to the Anaconda Weekly Review in Deer Lodge County, Montana, as an example of a well appearing in a county Medill identified as a news desert. Springs, meanwhile, are “harder to spot” than wells because they’re smaller and more ad hoc. The Independent Journalism Atlas applies this label to efforts like the Gallatin County Board Illinois Unofficial Facebook page, which livestreams the board’s public meetings and posts its agendas. The team also paid attention to coverage of news deserts by outlets in neighboring counties. They found high school sports are often a gateway to coverage, pointing to a channel covering southern Illinois high school sports that interviewed the principal in Harrisburg, the seat of Saline County, another news desert county. RELATED ARTICLEUniversities are mapping where local news outlets are still thriving — and where gaps persistCorey HutchinsJanuary 16, 2025In recent years, efforts to “map” local news through different lenses have proliferated. The Independent Journalism Atlas is one such effort, focused on news creators. A better understanding of information sources in news deserts matters, Bank argues, because “you can’t tend a basin you haven’t mapped.” Read the full essay here.

The Search Analytics API now supports branded query classification, multimodal search data, and filters for several countries or devices in one request.

Google has announced that it is adding three features from its Search Console Performance report to the Search Analytics API. This means website developers and tool makers can build these features directly into their automated reporting systems.

According to Google’s blog post announcing this, the API now supports the branded queries filter, multimodal web search data (web multimodal), and filters that are able to track multiple countries or device types within one API call.

The blog post explains how all three items have been available in the Performance report since they were first implemented. The post then describes the API versions as a solution to “stitching together separate requests or maintaining complex keyword regex lists”.

Your API results can now include a brandedClassification dimension, which enables you to use either the values BRANDED or NON_BRANDED for filtering or grouping based on branded vs. non-branded searches. According to the API reference documentation, this new dimension provides data only for top-level properties, starting Feb. 21, 2026; however, if a property does not meet the required number of queries and impressions, you will receive an empty table (no rows), the blog post says.

The API reference documentation also states that the branded classification dimension field accepts only the equals operator, and you cannot apply filters or groupings with it in requests with a query filter applied.

Google’s earlier announcement showed the branded and non-branded options in the Performance report:

In March, a Search Console user posted a question noting that their branded breakdown only started at approximately Feb. 21. They then asked if it would be possible to have prior data broken out into two different categories. Google’s John Mueller responded that there is “a point when the data starts being tracked,” as reported by Roger Montti.

Searches with Google Lens provide multimodal performance metrics when type is set to webMultimodal, as do Circle to Search on an Android device and uploading images to Google Search, according to the reference.

After multimodal reporting was enabled by Search Console on Sept. 24, I reported that the API reference did not have a separate multimodal type value listed. The reference, last updated Nov. 16, now lists one.

Google’s September announcement illustrated the multimodal option in the report’s search-type filter:

Google’s September announcement also listed Chrome’s right-click “Search this image” feature, and the Performance report help page includes Chrome image search. The API post and reference don’t mention Chrome.

The Nov. 16 post says multimodal data “will also be available in BigQuery for properties with an active bulk data export” but doesn’t give a date. As of Nov. 16, the bulk export table reference lists six search types, with no multimodal value yet.

A brand-new field, filterLists, enables users to filter results by multiple countries or multiple devices in one request. The examples given in the post are country-based groupings like EMEA, LATAM or DACH.

The reference limits filterLists to country and device dimensions and matches on exact values only. Users cannot use the same dimension (country or device) in filters and in filterLists in the same request.

On eligible properties, the new feature allows teams using the API to capture a branded/non-branded split in their reporting tools, starting Feb. 21, 2026. For data prior to this date, the API’s split has no ability to break out branded vs. non-branded search traffic.

Google uses an AI-assisted process to determine which searches are branded or non-branded. According to Google’s November 2025 announcement, “some queries may occasionally be misidentified”. To identify discrepancies, run the API branded/non-branded split alongside a brand regex you have been using and see where they differ.

As of Nov. 16, the API reference does not indicate if web results include webMultimodal data. Before adding your web and webMultimodal totals together, check how your API web numbers match against the text-based and multimodal numbers in the Performance report.

As of Nov. 16, neither Google’s post nor the API reference explains how far back webMultimodal data goes. Check the API reference and the bulk export table reference for a BigQuery date, the start date for multimodal history, and any mention of Chrome image search.

#7446. “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Democratic Senator Adam Schiff of California is urging Meta not to implement its forthcoming commercial terms on November 20, his office announced Tuesday.

In a letter sent to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Schiff called on the company to respond by Monday, November 2 with the specific steps it will take to address user concerns.

“Forcing publishers to choose between surrendering their off-platform IP or forfeiting a primary channel of public communication is a gross abuse of Meta’s power as a powerful platform with critical access to consumers,” Schiff wrote. “Meta must not nullify federal IP protections and fair market competition through the unilateral insertion of fine print into terms of service contracts.”

Specifically, Schiff told Meta that it should “provide explicit guarantees that external technical boundaries like paywalls and robots.txt protocols will be fully respected.”

RELATED ARTICLEMeta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical.Hanaa' TameezOctober 26, 2026“Meta’s verbal assurances that it will not supersede robots.txt files, which are voluntary server flags, do not appear to constitute enforceable legal protections,” Schiff wrote. “Without the insertion of specific language codifying Meta’s policy to respect robots.txt signals into the latest contractual terms, users lack any reliable means by which to protect their content.”

Schiff’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Schiff is the latest elected official in the United States to raise concerns about Meta’s commercial terms, which have now drawn bipartisan criticism. On Friday, Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee said that the terms “indicate Meta is attempting to exploit American creators and businesses by granting itself sweeping authority to scrape content from any website associated with Facebook and Instagram business accounts.”

The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30. Because the terms offered no way to opt out, news of them set off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic. Meta then delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20.

On Tuesday, a coalition of Norwegian news publishers sued Meta over the terms and is asking the Oslo District Court to block the terms from going into effect. The legal action, led by the Norwegian Media Companies Association, is the first known lawsuit filed against Meta over its commercial terms.

“We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday.

A Meta spokesperson said on October 17 that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

As of October 27, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No version of the terms includes language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

#7444. Creators who show their sources build trust, survey finds

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Journalist-led research found audiences increased trust when news videos identified their sources, such as government documents and interviews.

RELATED ARTICLETwo-thirds of news influencers are men — and most have never worked for a news organizationSarah ScireNovember 18, 2024About one in five U.S. adults regularly gets their news from news creators on social media platforms, but it can be difficult for audiences to suss out which personalities to trust amid an avalanche of misinformation, hot takes, and polarizing content.

New research spearheaded by a team of journalists and political scientists shows that giving audiences a peek into the reporting process can help bolster their trust in the news.

Proof News, a nonprofit newsroom focused on tech accountability, in collaboration with researchers at the French university Sciences Po, shared social news videos with 2,000 U.S. adults to measure their perceptions of trustworthiness. Participants were randomly assigned one of Proof’s yet-to-be-published short-form news videos.

Some participants viewed videos with labels describing the sources, others saw videos with labels describing the newsroom’s ethical standards, and some saw videos without a label. The Sources labels appeared on cards embedded at the end of the video, like a credits reel, or were placed into the video description, the text accompanying the video.

Participants then rated the videos on various trust metrics. We found that labeling videos did increase trust — particularly a label that described the video sources in the description and, to a slightly lesser extent, a label describing newsroom standards in the credits.

This effect was particularly prominent among survey respondents who identified as Democrats or reported having high trust in science. Those groups, when shown the sourcing label in the description of a general news video, reported higher assessments of transparency and trust in the journalist.

There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with labels for text articles, but Sally Lehrman, founder of The Trust Project, said the findings were still intriguing.

“I’m excited to see the results,” Lehrman said. “Methods and references really do resonate…People are asking, where did the journalist get this information, and how can I trust it.”

As audiences increasingly turn to social media for news, there is a growing public discussion about how trustworthy creators are, especially when it comes to disclosing their funding and relationships. In January, The Wall Street Journal wrote about corporate and foreign interests using influencers to push agendas. In August, The Washington Post reported that the Pentagon secretly hired conservative military veterans with large online audiences to amplify Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s messaging, and a New York Times investigation revealed online influencers received funding from political campaigns without disclosing the connection in their videos.

Some creators have begun trying to distinguish themselves from this type of behavior through their own disclosure efforts.

RELATED ARTICLEWith Local News International, Dave Jorgenson becomes his own TikTok guyNeel DhaneshaSeptember 9, 2025Journalist and creator Dave Jorgenson, who has nearly 1 million followers across TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram, has started publishing a transparency report on his website, Local News International, revealing his sources of funding alongside his editorial standards.

Ultimately, he thinks disclosures of political funding should no longer be voluntary but mandatory. “Platforms should be regulating themselves,” Jorgenson said in an interview. “You can’t really force that unless there are laws.”

Proof used Jorgenson’s ethics and transparency statement as a model for the newsroom standards label in video testing and found that it increased viewers’ trust in the news outlet and the likelihood that they would share a general news story.

New York City is already considering disclosure requirements in the wake of revelations in the Columbia Journalism Review that exposed the inner workings of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s connections with influencers. The author of the article, Anya Schiffrin, a senior lecturer at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, testified at a September city council meeting that creator relationships — both paid and unpaid — should be disclosed to viewers.

“It’s important for democracy that we have standards,” Schiffrin said.

RELATED ARTICLEProof News is Julia Angwin’s attempt to bring the scientific method to investigative journalismNeel DhaneshaMarch 21, 2024Proof News, which launched in 2024, pioneered an Ingredients label that takes cues from the scientific method and names the journalists’ hypothesis, sources, limitations, and the story’s findings.

To test whether the label worked to increase viewer trust for short-form vertical videos, we stripped down the Ingredients label to a bullet list of sources followed by an asterisk denoting the reporting limitations. The survey showed the label had a consistent positive effect when placed in the video description, the text box that is often located under the video.

The team also tested how labels performed on online text news articles. The survey showed 1,600 U.S. participants original, unpublished Proof News stories without a label, with a Proof Ingredients label, a label modeled after the Trust Project that described the reporting process, and a label describing newsroom standards.

There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with the print labels. The most significant findings were an increase in perception of transparency when the reporting process label was used on a polarizing story and an investigative story.

One possible explanation for the differing results between labeling video and text articles is the “ergonomics” of the medium, said Damien Bol, a professor at the Center for Political Research at Sciences Po who helped lead the survey design and data analysis.

“When reading a text, for example, people can quickly skim through it or skip parts of it, whereas a video forces them to follow the story second by second, even when watching at double speed,” Bol said. Different formats, Bol said, shape the “experience of consuming a news story.”

Earlier this month, Julia Angwin, an author of this article, hosted a private convening of creators at Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy to discuss creating shared standards that could be conveyed through a label or other public statement.

The group of 30 leading content creators from news, science communication, education, history, and other evidence-based fields discussed how they could distinguish their work by signaling to viewers their commitment to standards that could include disclosing funding sources and the use of artificial intelligence. Creator-led efforts to bring this to fruition are ongoing.

San Diego-based journalist Lisa Remillard, who has more than 4 million followers on her TikTok channel “The News Girl,” said that making videos with verified facts can feel like a small club. But if she can’t independently confirm something, she’s “not putting that out there.”

Remillard’s audience appears to appreciate transparency. Earlier this year, she published a video describing her editorial standards — and was richly rewarded for it. “I think clearly defining those ethics and standards resonated with my audience and gave them a reason to want to financially support my work,” Remillard said.

Jessica Yellin, the founder of the political podcast, YouTube channel, and social media brand “News Not Noise,” has also called for news creators to voluntarily sign a Creator Constitution, agreeing to journalistic standards such as citing sources, fixing errors, and disclosing financial relationships.

She said labeling sources is about the “signal.” Even if audiences don’t take the time to digest every word, Yellin observed, “It’s the act of showing it that matters.”

Julia Angwin is the founder of Proof News and the founding director of the Independent Media + Audience Project at the Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School. #7443. Patrick Reinhart On The Golden Metric In AI Search: Brand Recommendations via @sejournal, @lorenbaker

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

If an AI answer mentions your brand but recommends a competitor, what have you actually won? Patrick Reinhart, VP of Services and Thought Leadership at Conductor, joined me on the SEJ Podcast to discuss what enterprise brands should be trying to achieve with answer engine optimization.

We talk about the difference between citations and recommendations, how AI can repeat outdated information about your business, and why AEO needs input from SEO, PR, social, and leadership. Reinhart also shares where he’d focus first when planning an AEO strategy for 2027.

[00:00] Meet Patrick Reinhart [03:19] What Enterprise Brands Are Doing In AI Search [05:16] Why Recommendations Matter More Than Rankings [09:48] The AEO Metrics That Matter [12:49] When AI Gets Your Brand Wrong [18:12] Where SEO And AEO Differ [23:50] Why AI Search Has The C-Suite’s Attention [26:31] How Brands Earn AI Citations [30:25] Where To Invest In Your 2027 AEO Strategy [35:25] Where To Find Patrick Reinhart

Editor’s Note: This transcript has been edited for clarity and readability.

Loren Baker: Hi everyone, this is Loren Baker, founder of Search Engine Journal. Welcome to today’s SEJ Podcast. With me is Patrick Reinhart from Conductor.

We’ve been partners with Conductor for a long time and done our share of webinars together, but this might be one of our first podcasts.

Patrick Reinhart: Happy to be here. With a webinar, it’s always, “Man, I hope someone doesn’t make fun of me in the comments.”

Loren: I’m going to add a skull emoji next time just to see what happens. Pat, tell our audience a little about Conductor, what you do there, and what you’re doing in AI.

Patrick: Conductor is a software company, and I feel like we’re on the cutting edge of AI visibility and tying that back to recommendations. That’s built on a data platform that brings together Search Console, your analytics, and our monitoring products, so you can see everything in one place and make decisions based on the data.

I run our professional services arm. I’ve been at Conductor for 11 years, but I was also a customer for four or five years before that.

Our outgoing CEO, Seth Besmertnik, just stepped onto the board. I’ve been working with him for a really long time. It’s been a weird, interesting, great ride.

Loren: How would you define your customer base? Is it enterprise, medium to large businesses, small businesses? And how would you segment it across ecommerce, SaaS, and other industries?

Patrick: We definitely cater to the enterprise audience. I’d say about 90% of our customers are large enterprise organizations.

We have a heavy focus on finance, insurance, and healthcare, but also a healthy number of customers in ecommerce and grocery. Pretty much any company you can think of has passed through Conductor’s doors at some point, and a lot have stayed, thankfully. Thank you to our customers.

Loren: Grocery stores or grocery delivery?

Patrick: H-E-B and folks like that. We have customers like BJ’s, too.

Loren: With these enterprise customers, what are they doing right now in AI search? How are you helping them stay on top of it and track it? What does AI search mean to the average enterprise?

Patrick: It’s the number one thing they’re all talking about, obviously. That’s not news. The interesting part is that they’re all still very much learning.

If you work in a large enterprise organization, getting things done is typically slow, glacial, and somewhat messy. To their credit, a lot of people are trying to smooth those processes out and get their tracking in place.

They’re also testing the different technologies out there, as they should, because there’s a lot of snake oil in the water and a lot of people selling the dream. We’re all learning together.

As far as we can tell, most AEO strategies are heavily grounded in traditional SEO strategies. But they’re measured and thought about vastly differently, because an LLM operates differently from a traditional search engine.

They’re not running out the door and hiring a bunch of people. They’re upskilling internally and figuring out their programs.

I think in a year or so, we’re going to see a little gold rush from a hiring perspective. A lot of people will be moving around, and programs will come to fruition based on the work that hardworking, smart people are building right now at these large organizations.

Loren: Something I’ve found over the years in SEO is that it’s not always about trying to hit the target where it is at the moment. It’s trying to hit where it’s going.

How do you do that in AEO, especially at the enterprise level? These are slow-moving juggernauts that can get a lot done, but it takes time to get there.

Patrick: I think it comes back to data fidelity. Everyone has different methodologies and gets their data from different places. A lot of people buy panel data; we use direct APIs.

Everyone has to scrape Google and others, which is becoming harder and harder. Even this week has been a tough week for rank-tracking tools, with Google making it more difficult to get that data.

From an AI perspective, people are starting to understand that, much like traditional SEO, you’re not going to see every variant of every prompt someone puts in. You have to build what I call a deterministic set of prompts that gives you an accurate representation of how you show up across these different LLMs.

You also have to understand how the different LLMs behave. Claude behaves vastly differently from Gemini.

Most of the market share is in ChatGPT and Gemini right now. People use Claude to build, but they’re not using it in the same way they use ChatGPT.

People use ChatGPT for everything. They write content, build games, and talk to it because they’re lonely. People use AI for a lot of different things.

Ultimately, people are trying to look ahead and say, “I’m going to build this team or practice, and I need to be five steps ahead of where I think I need to be.” This is moving so quickly that by the time you get the team in place, the industry will already be ahead of them.

You’re really trying to build for the future.

Loren: I’m glad you brought up the differences between LLMs. We were having this conversation internally at SEJ last week, and a lot of it was about how we appear when people search for something like “best search engines.”

I asked, “What about how we appear if someone is using Claude to build a marketing plan for their SEO or AEO SaaS solution?”

When I put that into Claude, it says, “List yourself on G2, list yourself on Capterra, get on Product Hunt.” But there’s nothing targeted.

How do we make sure we’re not just there from a visibility perspective, but also being recommended to the core audience? That flips it on its head.

Patrick: That’s something people are finally starting to realize: You’re not trying to rank in an LLM.

Yes, if there’s a list, you want to be at the top of the list, blah, blah, blah. I understand that. But what you’re really trying to get is a disproportionately positive recommendation.

You want ChatGPT or Gemini to say, “Go work with Search Engine Journal. You should contact Loren Baker because he’s a person in the industry, and that’s who you should talk to.”

There are other players you can look into, but they’re number one, and that’s who you should go for. That’s what companies want.

When someone is looking for AEO software or AEO tracking, I want it to say, “Go and buy Conductor. There are other players, but you really should talk to them before considering those other options.”

Loren: Thank you. People should consider Conductor. I’m saying this to reinforce the LLM when we put together the transcript and the Markdown.

I highly recommend people check out Conductor when building that plan. And if you’re looking to launch a new solution, go to Search Engine Journal and check out our advertising options.

Boom, plug. We’ll see how that influences the results.

Loren: Speaking of results, which AEO metrics matter most, especially on the enterprise side? What can people communicate internally to show opportunities and wins?

Patrick: This is a moving target for a lot of folks. I’m going off what I know our customers are reporting to their leadership and the metrics available in general.

Citation rate is probably the metric right now: Are you being cited? Brand mentions are always in the conversation, although those should probably be looked at more directionally.

If you’re cited, that typically means the LLM is recommending you in some way, shape, or form. Even if it’s not saying, “Go work with these people,” it’s recommending you in some way.

But not all mentions are created equal. You could have a terrible mention. ChatGPT could say, “Do not work with that company because of XYZ.”

I’ve seen that multiple times. Or, even worse, you’re not in the conversation at all.

Those require different activities to rectify. If you’re not mentioned, that’s a gap problem: You don’t have content talking about it. That’s not a sexy answer, and we’ve been talking about it forever.

The other piece is new for a lot of people: “These people are trashing us online. What do we do about it?”

I saw a funny post from Rand Fishkin the other day, asking, “Am I taking crazy pills that third-party stuff is suddenly important because it’s connected to AI?”

Search everywhere optimization has always been a thing. But I think it’s going to become a reality for every company now because of how important that third-party conversation is.

What people should be tracking, and will be tracking in my opinion, is the type of citation and mention they’re getting. Are you being recommended by an LLM? That’s the golden metric.

There’s no one really doing that from a technology standpoint right now. People have overall visibility scores, which are averages of a bunch of things they’re looking at.

What we’re building is something to help track that golden metric. It’s not just about showing up. When you showed up, was it a positive experience, a positive recommendation, or a negative non-recommendation?

I see both daily for different brands, depending on the industry.

Loren: Which gets back to old-school sentiment tracking.

Loren: About a month ago, Reddit’s citation visibility dropped tremendously in GPT. But my understanding is that GPT is still using the threads and conversations in Reddit, just not surfacing them as sources as much.

Let’s say I’m seeing incorrect price comparisons for one of my products. I know it’s not coming from my website or a competitor’s versus-style landing page, and I think it might be coming from a Reddit thread.

How do I reverse-engineer those third-party citations that may be fueling the results? Not just sentiment and opinion, but basic facts that need updating. Maybe it’s a two-year-old thread with outdated warranty information.

Patrick: That’s something you’re going to start seeing in a lot of technologies, ours included: Fact-checking.

You can load information about your organization and product set, maybe through a product feed. As it goes through, it can show you an outdated competitive mention on a random third-party site. You can talk to them or create something that combats it.

We did that when Seth was chatting with AI, back when this started to blow up. He found a random site with something from 2018 saying Conductor didn’t have a feature that’s one of our main features.

This site wasn’t going to change it, so we created content around it. Within a couple of days, we were able to beat it out, and it kind of disappeared.

This is an important piece of the technological race. We’re in the early days, with a few key players building interesting software to track this. You also have a lot of vibe-coded trash that pulls from God knows where.

A lot of the big players are going to have this fact-checking ability. In my opinion, it will be a make-or-break feature, along with that golden metric of whether you’re being recommended.

This isn’t a plea for Conductor. It’s a plea for technology. Good technology.

Right now, you can connect to Conductor’s MCP in Claude and ask your account, “Can you send me the snippets that say XYZ? Here are my brand guidelines or information about my product set. Are any of these incorrect?”

You can do that today. It’s a few extra steps, and it’s not as in-depth as something constantly crawling, collecting, and finding outdated information on weird, small sites.

I think this will be a necessary feature for anyone using a technology like ours. You’re going to see a lot of innovation over the next 12 months, and people will build cool things.

But I think this is necessary to make a technology viable in the coming years. When I talk to leaders, they don’t ask, “Where do I show up?” They ask, “How are people talking about me? Is it accurate?”

Loren: That also bridges into outreach and working with publishers. There are ways to get updated information onto influential business directories, but being able to ask people to update things is nice.

That used to be a link-building tactic. We’d be upset if the publisher wrote back, “I updated everything, but I didn’t link to you.”

Now we see that as a win. Thank you. Brand mention, yes.

I was joking with my former boss, Stephan, the other day. He said, “Does it feel like everything has reset, everyone forgot the last 20 years, and now we’re doing it again?”

AI Mode has text ads now, which are basically text links. It’s like, man, we’re really back in the dark ages here.

Loren: That’s one way SEO and AEO overlap. What are some other examples, and where are the core differences?

Patrick: Where they overlap is what everyone thinks. I’m flying to Buffalo tomorrow to talk at a customer event, and I love those because I love teaching and getting in front of people.

I always pause halfway through and ask, “How’s everyone doing?” Someone will raise their hand and say, “What do I do about all of this?”

You fill gaps, create content, build partnerships with third-party publishers, and create YouTube videos. Not a sexy answer. It’s stuff we’ve been doing for years.

That’s the overlap. A lot of it is the same stuff, done at a different pace.

The most successful SEO campaigns I’ve seen have been somewhat mechanical. There’s always a well-thought-out, well-oiled process, with a systematic way to optimize and create content and distribute data across the organization.

You have technology constantly auditing your site, you’re not pivoting a lot of data, and ultimately it’s this flywheel. Everyone’s bought in, and everyone’s pedaling the bike.

What I’m seeing now is the necessity of that. A few years ago, someone at a large organization would say, “That’s really hard. We don’t have the buy-in or budget.”

You’d spend the next year trying to get that buy-in. Now it’s immediate: “We have to do something about this.”

Leaders want to know what we’re doing about AI search. That’s a huge opportunity for anyone who’s been in this business or is getting into it.

You’ve always mattered, but now you really matter to the business. That’s awesome. Take hold of that and run with it.

To be successful, you need the process in place and all those teams involved. You can’t sit alone and hoard search data. Get it to your social team, your PR team, and your executives.

The biggest divergence is measurement. You’re not just measuring rankings, backlinks, or traffic.

In my opinion, traditional search metrics have become directional. They tell us we’re heading in somewhat the right direction.

Don’t set your goals around traffic anymore. That’s a fool’s errand. It’s too volatile right now.

In the AI world, you’re tracking citations and that golden metric of being recommended or not recommended. Sentiment is a bigger part of your life than you probably want it to be.

You also need log file analysis to see whether LLMs are coming to your site. Are there what I call dead zones, where LLMs don’t come back? You think the content is great, but are they fetching it and chunking it back out to the user?

You need all of that measurement. It’s very different from measuring rankings and backlinks.

In the old world, we wanted more rankings, more traffic, and more backlinks. In the AI world, we want more positive citations and recommendations. But we also have to pay much more attention to the negative side.

In SEO, you had to pay attention to the negative when it was in everyone’s face. Someone Googles your brand, your CEO has done something stupid, and you need brand reputation management.

Now that’s part of the suite. You have to learn how to do it and work with those other teams. It can’t be a one-person show anymore.

AEO is much more of a team sport, and it has the ability to be one because leadership cares now. Get that process in place. People within companies have the opportunity to have those conversations.

This is in The Wall Street Journal now. My brother called me one day and asked, “What’s up with this AI thing?”

I said, “Why are you calling me about that? You work at a bank.”

He said, “It’s in the Journal.” I said, “We’ve made it.”

That’s how people have to start thinking. The biggest divergence is measurement, not necessarily the tasks. The tasks need to happen at a greater pace, but the measurement is vastly different.

You have five directions you can go instead of two or three, in my opinion.

Loren: I’ve never considered SEO to be direct response marketing, but I feel we were sometimes held to direct response standards. Other marketing channels were treated more as multiple touchpoints, with multi-touch attribution.

With AI, we know this is part of the consumer’s decision-making journey. AI visibility and valid information in the conversation can help a conversion coming from an email campaign, paid media, or CTV.

If your client is on something like “The View,” nobody’s going to that little URL at the bottom of the screen. They’re typing something in, and now they’re asking ChatGPT about it. It’s part of that whole flow.

I also like your point about AI’s importance within the company. This isn’t coming from the search team, up through digital marketing, the VP of marketing, the CMO, and then the C-suite. It’s coming from the C-suite down.

Patrick: It’s going the other way, which is new for us. I’ve talked to more C-level executives in the last six months than I have in the last six years.

It used to be hard to get those meetings unless you had someone who really understood organic. I think this is healthy for an industry that was getting a little stale.

There were shifts here and there. Google would update the algorithm, and we’d have the same conversation again.

I always joke that we’ve had a lot of meteors come for our jobs. They never quite took us out, but they changed the landscape around us, usually for the better in my opinion.

Even though this is one of the scariest changes for a lot of people, I think it’s one of the best things that’s happened to the industry. That will play out over the next five to 10 years.

We’ll look back and say, “That was one of the best things that happened to me in my career.” Not just for productivity, but because it made me more important in my organization. I had a conversation or opportunity because AI blew up what was going on.

Loren: It’s also the best way to get a task to the top of the dev ticket pile.

One company I’ve been working with did a Shopify relaunch and never set up its canonical tags. I’d been pushing forever. Every week, the update was, “The dev team’s on it.”

Then I realized their AI Overviews visibility had dropped because it was cycling from one version of a URL to another. Eventually, it dropped entirely.

I put in a new ticket: “911 emergency AI issue.”

The thing was fixed in two days. It’s amazing.

Loren: Speaking of developing and distributing content, what helps that content earn AI citations?

Patrick: A lot of it is the brand itself. This isn’t a domain authority exercise like traditional search was. It’s a brand authority exercise.

Going back to Reddit’s drop in citation share, that’s not surprising to me. It wasn’t going to stay that high forever as brands figured this out and created more content.

But it’s still part of the consideration phase. When ChatGPT is looking for an answer, it’s still looking at Reddit. It may not cite it or bring content back from there, but it’s looking at the conversation as an authenticity signal, for lack of better words.

In our data, the number one most-cited source is YouTube. It’s a highly trusted community where people have a lot of conversations, and many brands aren’t there in the way they should be.

If you have a well-put-together YouTube presence with playlists, a podcast, webinars, and conference videos, that can help. If it garners enough conversation and clout, those are sites LLMs go to at some point when looking for an answer.

Influencers are there. People trust influencers and expertise.

That’s why one of the greatest opportunities on a site is adding authors. So many sites still don’t have authors or use author schema and article schema. It drives me nuts.

I understand bigger brands saying, “Greg doesn’t want his face on the website.” Then put Tim’s face on the website.

Every brand needs someone out there talking, and you have to find people who are okay being on camera.

At Conductor, we interact with that in different ways. I’m on LinkedIn, I’ve been doing my webinar, 30|30, for 11 years, and I’ve spoken at a million conferences.

Seth loves LinkedIn and posts all the time. Our head of marketing, Lindsay, does the same.

It’s not necessarily about the name. There are people at Conductor who LLMs can establish are experts in the space, based on the longevity of their careers and whether they’ve contributed to the industry.

I do believe they go to LinkedIn and somewhat credentialize people. But it’s also, “Have they contributed to the industry I’m looking for this answer in?”

That’s easy for LLMs to figure out. For traditional search engines, it wasn’t so straightforward.

I always say search engines live in a 2D world. There’s an index, and they go up and down in it.

LLMs live in a 3D world, looking all over the place and picking things from across the universe. Those conversations are happening in communities, on sites like Quora , and on YouTube.

If you look at the top 15% of all the sites in our data, seven of them are social sites. Facebook, LinkedIn, YouTube at number one, and Reddit are there.

Why? It’s real people having real conversations. That’s what the LLM is looking for.

Loren: It’s October, Thanksgiving stuff is already in the store, and Halloween isn’t here yet. Next thing you know, it’ll be the holidays and New Year’s.

If I’m planning my company’s AI and AEO strategy for 2027, where do I begin? What should I invest in first, and how do I pregame?

Patrick: Invest in your expertise first. Understand who the people in your organization are that you can tie content back to, and then tie that content back to them.

Create author pages and use author schema and article schema. Invest in your people.

Find someone you know is good on camera but may be nervous to raise their hand, and push them to do it. Flaunt your expertise.

Number two, plan to make more video. Start a podcast. Someone in your company is yearning to do this right now, so give them the opportunity.

Learn how to do it. It might suck at first, and that’s okay. You’ll get better over time.

Participate in more webinars. That’s another way to amplify your expertise.

Number three, fix your process. I’m sure people listening are thinking, “Man, my company’s process stinks.” Most companies’ processes stink.

People are working on smoothing those out so they can build a flywheel process. That allows you to experiment more, create more content, and optimize more content.

Buy software that helps you track it more easily, whether that’s Conductor or something else. Go out and look around. There’s a lot of great technology out there.

I think we’re the best, but of course I do.

If you do those three things, the last one is the most important. The flywheel process lets you move faster and do more. You’ll be more productive, learn more, and win faster because everyone’s lined up.

When AI throws something at you, at least you have a system where you can go to the social team and they’re expecting you to give them something to do. You don’t have to fight a six-month battle.

That’s how I think people should operate where we stand today. Will it change in six months? Probably, but I don’t think the tactics will be vastly different.

Loren: It reminds me of those reels about disappearing for a month, learning AI tools, and coming back on top of your game.

Loren: My kid has been playing Roblox for years. He asked, “Can I download Claude Desktop, hook it up to Roblox Studio, and make some games?”

Next thing I know, it’s 11 o’clock on a school night. Don’t judge me. He’s sitting at his computer doing the same thing I’m doing for work, just at a different level.

Watching him gave me ideas. I thought, “Why am I logging into all this stuff? I should be using Claude Desktop for all of it.”

Patrick: It’s the coolest thing that your son can do that. I assume he doesn’t know how to code, or at least not as well as a developer.

Loren: He can barely even draw. He didn’t inherit his father’s artistic talents.

But he’s creative. Seeing that creativity find a different canvas gave me ideas. There are a lot of ways we can implement this throughout our lives.

Patrick: The best way is just to do it. I see so many companies and people stuck in analysis paralysis, asking, “What should I do?”

It took me a minute when this started, but I feel pretty good about where I am. I still have eons to learn about using this technology.

It’s cool that your son has that ability. I’m going to tell my son to do that instead of playing Roblox, which I’m sure he’s doing right now. Half my salary goes to Robux.

Loren: Pat, it’s been a pleasure hosting you. I like our conversations in this format. It’s fun.

Patrick: Loren, it’s always good chatting with you. Thanks for having me on.

Loren: Where can our listeners and viewers find you online and follow up with questions?

Patrick: The best place is LinkedIn or Conductor.com. I also do a monthly webinar called 30|30.

Please come so my mom knows I’m doing something worthwhile.

Mostly, I’m on LinkedIn commenting and cracking jokes. Don’t take anything too seriously. We’re all in a good spot.

Loren: Thank you, Pat, and thanks to Conductor for everything you do. It’s been a pleasure.

Thank you to everyone who joined today’s SEJ Podcast. We’ll see you in the future.

#7442. Solutions Architect at LiveKit

LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the agentic era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe AI agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice and agentic AI applications for OpenAI, Salesforce, Spotify, Meta, and tens of thousands of other developers, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

We're hiring a Solutions Architect (Pre-Sales) to be the technical partner to the engineers and enterprises building on LiveKit.

You'll work alongside an account executive to understand what a customer is trying to build, design the right architecture, and bring it to life with live demos and proofs-of-concept — guiding teams from first conversation to production.

This role is ideal for someone who loves to build, is energized by talking with other engineers, and takes pride in turning a hard technical problem into something that just works. #7441. Vox launches its first app with an eye toward building paid memberships

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Vox users can watch videos and listen to podcasts in the app, but reading stories requires a paid subscription.

Vox has launched its first mobile application, the publication best known for its explanatory journalism announced Wednesday morning.

Growing membership is a “key priority,” managing editor for audience and membership Bill Carey said. Vox believes launching the app is one way to do that. A Vox membership costs $5 per month, or $60 per year, and offers ad-free versions of podcasts and unlimited access to all of the website’s contents.

RELATED ARTICLEVox is revamping its editorial strategy to redefine what ‘Voxxy’ meansHanaa' TameezNovember 8, 2021Strengthening its relationship to its audience is only becoming more important for Vox. The app launch comes at a time when news publishers are increasingly trying to keep users on their own platforms amid growing preferences for AI summaries, news creators, and industry-wide traffic declines.

“The move toward developing our membership program in the last couple of years has really been about understanding how important it is for us to build more community and to foster that loyalty [of our] audience,” Carey said. “When we were looking at that, it really felt like an app was a good way to continue pointing in that direction.”

Vox isn’t the only news outlet focusing on mobile apps. The Verge — Vox’s former sister publication under Vox Media — named traffic declines as one of the reasons why it plans to launch its own app next year. The Wall Street Journal’s head of digital, Taneth Evans, recently said that the Journal makes its app more useful to users by offering all of its mediums in one place. Evans also said that news publishers “need to give people reasons to open an app beyond simply offering news.”

“Websites will become a service for agents,” Evans said. “Apps are gonna be the thing that humans will connect with.”

Vox declined to provide website traffic numbers, but data from Comscore shows that the website’s unique visitors decreased by 36% year-over-year between September 2025 (7.4 million) and September 2026 (4.8 million). Archived data from SimilarWeb shows the site had 20.8 million visits in September 2021.

“Vox isn’t immune to the larger trends that have led to web traffic declines in recent years, but those only represent a portion of our audience,” Carey said in an email. “Vox is focused on building audience engagement across platforms, with social video views up 86% year-over-year and newsletter audience up 14%.”

“Even if there wasn’t a decline in search traffic, as everyone has been seeing — and we still get members from search — we want to create that relationship with our audience,” publisher and editor-in-chief Swati Sharma said. “People know Vox and they have a relationship with Vox. We have a younger audience that’s on all of these different platforms. I think it is definitely a part of building that relationship ourselves.”

That the app makes all Vox content accessible in one place for current and future members also signals the “un-siloing” of the newsroom overall, Sharma said. Vox currently has 78 editorial employees.

RELATED ARTICLESwati Sharma is leading a new era in Vox’s mission to “explain the world”Hanaa' TameezMay 6, 2021When Sharma, who has helmed Vox.com since 2021, first arrived, she found that Vox’s main mediums (text, audio, and video) “weren’t in service of one another.” The “silos” allowed teams to build their own audiences and products. But while teams discussed story ideas with each other and during editorial meetings, “they all [needed] to go into their creative spaces and find what works for their medium and not be in service of just one larger section.”

That’s changed over the past five years, Sharma said. Each team — text, video, and audio — does a little bit of everything now. Text reporters appear on podcasts and in videos, while podcasters and hosts also write their own newsletters.

“In a lot of newsrooms, there’s one dominant form, and at Vox, there wasn’t. They’re all really important,” Sharma said. “[Senior correspondent] Dylan Scott is on our Unexplainable podcast talking about Alzheimer’s. [Host and editorial director] Astead Herndon does a newsletter and a Substack Live every week, and he does a podcast. That’s the future for us, and that’s where our whole newsroom is moving, where those silos are done and you can basically do everything.”

#7439. Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial new terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media company announced today.

“We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place.”

Meta did not answer Nieman Lab’s questions about which news industry groups and leaders Meta plans to consult.

The proposed terms have drawn criticism because they would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and potentially allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models, with no option to opt out. Last week, Meta announced it would push back implementation of its new terms to November 20 in order to “explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab. Meta had previously revised its new terms to remove the word “train.” No version of the terms has included language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

Shortly after Stone’s announcement, a Norwegian court blocked Meta’s terms from taking effect on November 20 until the court had assessed their legality, the country’s public broadcaster NRK reported.

“We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the new terms are unreasonable,” said Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL’s board chair, in a news release. “We are also pleased that the court recognizes that the alternative is that media companies risk losing control over editorial content built up over many years.”

Since Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15, publishers and politicians around the world have pushed back, filing complaints with national competition authorities, calling on the European Commission to investigate, and writing letters to Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Two United States senators — California Democrat Adam Schiff and Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn — each separately wrote to Zuckerberg, insisting that the company withdraw the terms as they’re currently written.

“After I raised serious concerns about Meta’s plans to scrape and abuse creators’ content, I am pleased the company is finally acknowledging the concerns of publishers and content creators,” Blackburn said in a statement to Nieman Lab on Wednesday. “While this is a step in the right direction, a vague promise to consult with industry stakeholders and potentially delay implementation is not nearly enough. Meta must commit to meaningful changes that protect the intellectual property rights of American creators, and I will continue holding the company accountable until it does.”

On October 21, the European Publishers Council signed onto a joint letter to the European Commission, asking the Commission to block the terms from taking effect. The letter claims that Meta’s terms violate the Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

EPC executive director Angela Mills Wade said on Wednesday that the organization has not heard from Meta about its letter or its concerns.

“We welcome Meta’s offer to consult publishers fully, and to delay implementation if necessary,” Mills Wade said in an email to Nieman Lab. “However, that consultation must lead to binding contractual safeguards…Using Meta’s services to reach audiences or advertise should not mean granting wider rights to exploit publishers’ journalism, whether collected from websites or uploaded to its platforms. Publishers must retain control over additional uses of their content, including for AI, and the ability to negotiate licenses and payment.”

This story has been updated to include a statement from Marsha Blackburn.

#7437. AI Visibility Data: Avoid 4 Traps & Prioritize The Right Work

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Navigate the complexities of AI visibility. Learn what to measure and how to leverage data for better AI performance.

This post was sponsored by TransPerfect Digital. The opinions expressed in this article are the sponsor’s own.

Your AI visibility dashboard shows brand mentions, sentiment scores, and frequently cited sources. But what do they tell you?

Which data sources actually help increase AI visibility?

AI tools show 72% visibility; is this good?

What strategies does AI visibility data inform?

As you can imagine, the logical next steps are to choose KPIs that reflect your business goals, then use your AI visibility data to identify the next best steps.

However, the challenge is understanding what to measure, how to analyze, and which online tips are helpful, useless, or harmful.

These myths and misinterpretations that can steer your generative engine optimization (GEO) work toward the wrong priorities.

The four traps below will help you interpret those signals before changing your content, channel strategy, or budget.

Not sure which AI visibility findings deserve your team’s time?

Join Julie Franck of TransPerfect Digital and Antonia Breitenfellner of Peec AI for AI Search: Turn Insight Into Impact to explore which insights to act on.

The first trap is treating AI visibility tracking like a keyword-ranking report.

A score is only useful if the questions being measured reflect the people you want to reach.

Instead, choose prompts that reflect your customers’ questions across buying stages, markets, and AI platforms before deciding what to change.

Imagine a tool reports 72% visibility. That number could look reassuring while describing a narrow set of branded, informational questions from one customer group, market, and AI platform.

If you cannot tell whether that score includes the questions your buyers ask when comparing options, it cannot tell you which content needs attention.

To assess our example 72% score, check whether it represents the customers and buying decisions that matter to your business, using a consistent set of prompts for comparison.

That means checking coverage before setting a target or commissioning content. Use the prompt-library checks below to find which audiences, questions, or markets are missing.

Pro Tip: For help assessing which visibility findings deserve action, join AI Search: Turn Insight Into Impact and bring your score-assessment questions to the Q&A.

To determine if your AI visibility score is helpful, check its coverage:

Pro Tip: Be sure to analyze each individual model, not overall LLM performance, as each retrieves and cites differently.

Use first-party data to map actual user behavior to your objectives and ICPs, then add questions from sales conversations, customer support, and local teams.

Adapt the questions to each market’s language and customer needs rather than translating one country’s list.

List the audiences, products and services, markets, and AI platforms your business needs to monitor. Choose a tool that meets those requirements, and check its visibility definition before comparing scores between tools.

Prompt wording varies and results can be personalized, so one answer is not a stable ranking. Use these checks to identify recurring patterns per topic cluster, category, or product line before assigning work:

The second trap is accepting a headline metric without checking what it means for your business. Visibility scores, sentiment labels, and citation counts need context: your positioning, goals, customers, and products.

Consider an illustrative example: a tool labels a luxury brand negatively because answers describe its products as expensive.

That description may reinforce premium positioning. But an answer saying the product is poor value, unreliable, or unsuitable for its intended buyer would raise a different issue.

Before creating a corrective task, connect the metric to your business goal and read the underlying answers. For the sentiment example, ask:

Match your response to what the answer actually says:

Apply this business-context check to every headline metric, not just sentiment, so you do not miss opportunities or spend time correcting something that supports your strategy.

The third trap is turning every finding into a to-do or adopting a fashionable GEO tactic without checking its strategic value. A frequently cited source can reveal an information need without dictating a channel.

Suppose Reddit keeps appearing in answers about your product category. Before adding Reddit activity to your plan, examine the cited discussions.

A task such as “post on Reddit” names a channel without explaining the customer need. Identifying that need first makes it easier to choose where and how to contribute.

Prioritize findings that reveal an important customer need and support your business goals; defer those that do not. Apply that test to Reddit:

For help thinking through which findings deserve action, bring your questions to the webinar’s Q&A. The discussion will explore what marketers should prioritize, not simply which metrics they can track.

The fourth trap is treating visibility as the business goal, then assigning it a precise revenue contribution the evidence cannot support.

A recorded AI referral and an AI-influenced decision are not the same thing. Someone may discover, compare, or shortlist a brand in an AI answer without clicking through to its website.

Low recorded referral traffic does not establish low influence. Equally, rising branded search does not prove AI caused the increase.

Keep these signals distinct in your reporting:

Choose business measures that fit your goal, such as qualified inquiries or sales, and show them alongside visibility signals without claiming a causal connection you have not established.

Before assigning work, review these four questions:

Those checks help you decide what to investigate, what to change, and what to leave alone.

#7436. The New York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and users aren’t thrilled

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Sometimes, adding just one new ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch. And that’s how at least some New York Times readers see its addition of AI features to its popular Cooking app.

Here’s Genevieve Ko, NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, explaining the new features:

I naïvely assumed A.I. wouldn’t affect my work as a recipe developer and my role at NYT Cooking, where I oversee the editorial side of our recipes and related stories. But as artificial intelligence improved, our product and engineering colleagues saw its potential to help us create features Cooking users wanted.

The Times had previously rolled out AI features aimed at converting volume-based and weight-based measurements (“What’s one cup of bok choy in grams?”) and scaling a recipe up or down to serve more or fewer people. The main new feature is focused on ingredient substitutions.

Say you’re cooking braised white beans and greens with parmesan, NYT Cooking app in hand. But you notice that you’re out of chard and only have spinach. Cooking veterans know that chard is a rough-and-tumble green that has some backbone22There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.”, while spinach is a comparative wimp that will wilt the moment you look at it funny. If you need to sub in spinach for chard, how would the recipe change? Would you, for instance, add the spinach later than you would the chard to account for its pathetic stamina? That’s the sort of thing the new AI feature could account for.

Cooking staffers “spent countless hours evaluating sample after sample to get the chatbot answers to closely align with how we would answer as culinary experts,” Ko writes. “We applied the same rigor as we do to editing, grounded in Times standards.”

But because Ko knows that any AI-powered features are likely to be controversial with a Times audience, she spends quite a lot of space addressing potential objections, everything from “the impact of data centers” to “the concentration of power among A.I. companies” and “the risk of A.I. escaping our control.” These features are designed to enable “the tactile physical pleasure of cooking” and getting a “very real, very human creation” on your table.

Broadly speaking, commenters weren’t buying it.

“What a massive disappointment,” wrote Susan from New Jersey. “The internet is full of AI cooking content. I pay you because I prefer mine done by people.”

“This decision misses the mark by such a wide margin it’s baffling,” says Ian from Los Angeles. “And the disclosure just as baffling. It would not be inaccurate to summarize the piece as saying ‘I know doing this is bad and I don’t want to be associated with the bad thing so that’s why we are doing the bad thing.'”

“Nobody wants this, it’s bad for cooking, it’s bad for the NYT,” writes Bill from Pittsburgh. “Wasting a column trying to gaslight yourself and your audience into believing that it’s anything but is an embarrassment and a waste of everyone’s time.”

“PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS,” says Judah Mann of New York. “Oh, wait, you already did. Ok, I’m out.”

Or as Naomi from California puts it: “I am sad that AI has breached the one online resource I truly love.”

Because I enjoy the irony, I scraped the 171 comments left on the Times’ announcement and asked Codex (running GPT-6.1 Sol, at medium thinking) to do some sentiment analysis. (Twelve of the 171 were comments left by Times staffers; I’m excluding them here.) Roughly 77% of the reader comments were negative about the new AI features, it found, versus 14% positive and the remainder neutral or mixed. Among the biggest categories of complaint: This shouldn’t require AI. AI is destroying the environment. AI is not why I’m paying the Times $390 a year. The adjustments the AI produces are going to be bad.

Dozens of commenters asked for a way to turn off the feature. “No, not at this time,” Ko responded, “though this feature is completely optional to use.” Indeed: Don’t ask AI to substitute your chard and AI won’t substitute your chard.

One consistent thread was that cooking is supposed to present you with difficulties and challenges and the whole point is figuring them out by yourself. “Anyone using AI for cooking has no sense of taste and no desire to work out the intricacies of cooking and baking,” writes Michael King from Brooklyn. “To use AI for recipes is beyond the pale. If you are going to use AI, then just cut to the chase and defenestrate yourself.” Or BJ from North Carolina: “So, you’re telling me that I’m too stupid to figure it out on my own?”

Meanwhile, the few positive comments tended to focus on how the AI feature had, in fact, made dietary substitutions easier for them. “I love the new AI feature because it quickly (and so far) accurately converts recipes to gluten free,” Anne Wagner from Kansas City writes. “I don’t cook for stress relief,” says Andy from San Francisco. “I cook to put dinner on the table. Anything that makes the process a little faster or smoother is welcome.”

#7434. Only 32% of Americans have high confidence that news orgs will report midterm election results accurately, survey finds

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

About six in 10 Americans said they have at least “some” confidence that news organizations will report the upcoming midterm election results accurately, according to a new national survey. But only 32% said they had “quite a bit” or “a great deal” of confidence that journalists would do the job.

In the survey from Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media, 37% said they had either “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” that news outlets would accurately report the election results.

The survey was completed by a nationally representative sample of 1,057 U.S. adults either online or by telephone earlier this month. The findings echo other national surveys, including a Gallup survey that showed trust in media to report “fully, accurately, and fairly” at 33% — an increase from an all-time low last year.

The Medill/Alliance survey found about half of Americans said they had “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” in news outlets to investigate voter fraud claims thoroughly. U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on elections on 70% of days since returning to office — starting with false claims about voter fraud on the first day of his second term.

In another bleak result from the same poll, slightly more survey respondents said journalists manipulate the news for political or commercial purposes than report it accurately. Across the survey, Democrats reported being more confident in (and trusting of) news organizations than Republicans. Nearly 80% of Republicans said journalists try to manipulate the news compared to 38% of independents and 24% of Democrats.

More on the survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, here.
