#7372. Seals, construction, and midterms drive traffic gains at Massachusetts nonprofit news outlets

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

At Cambridge Day, “having full-time reporters was transformative.” Our latest traffic rankings for nonprofit news outlets.

Is something in the water in Nieman Lab’s home state? In our latest quarterly ranking of nonprofit news outlets, eight Massachusetts nonprofit news outlets enjoyed significant jumps in traffic. Massachusetts is the state that appeared most frequently in this quarter’s data, followed by California (7), Michigan (4), and New York (4).

Four of those Massachusetts outlets largely attributed the traffic spikes to hyperlocal stories that served specific reader needs and curiosities.

Cambridge Day garnered 160,000 visits in July, a 60% increase from June. Editor Michael Fitzgerald (a 2011 Nieman Fellow) said the publication’s top story that month was about the city halting a multifamily home demolition. Other big stories covered the sale of two independent movie theaters and a July 4 shooting.

Reader support allowed Cambridge Day to hire a full-time reporter in June, along with four summer intern reporters whose positions were funded through their universities. In July, Fitzgerald said, the news outlet published 32 stories per week.

“Having full-time reporters was transformative. News does not pay a living wage to freelancers,” Fitzgerald said in an email. “They have to pay their bills by doing other things, so they just aren’t as available as full-time reporters. We made the decision to hire a second reporter, who started in late August. We took a bit of a risk and brought on [a] freelancer as a six-month editorial fellow. I cut my freelance budget in half and have rejiggered some other expenses to make this less risky.”

The Lexington Observer got 62,000 visits in August, a 47% increase from the previous month. Executive director Lauren Feeney said the August story with the most traffic was about how a resident-led complaint delayed the construction of what would be the most expensive high school in the country.

Election coverage ahead of the midterms also resonated. “Our coverage of two little-known progressive candidates running to unseat [Rep. Katherine Clark] from the left got a ton of traffic, I believe because hardly anything else had been written about them, so readers came to our site not just from Lexington but from the entire 5th Congressional district, including Cambridge,” Feeney said. “My takeaway from this is to keep focusing on undercovered and hyperlocal stories, and not spend a lot of resources on stories that are already widely covered.”

August was also a newsy month for the Marblehead Current. With 156 published stories in August, the Current’s traffic increased by 53% compared to July. Cofounder and reporter Leigh Blander said her investigation into the city’s road conditions sparked engagement on Facebook and Instagram, driving pageviews. Other stories that resonated with readers covered a boat crash, a seal carcass, racist graffiti, and education coverage during back-to-school season.

CommonWealth Beacon, which covers statewide politics and policy, saw its September traffic increase by 37% over August. Editor Laura Colarusso attributed the growth to the publication’s coverage of Massachusetts’ nine ballot questions.

“Our ballot question guide brought a lot of new readers to our site and strengthened our relationship with many of the hyperlocal news organizations that regularly republish our stories,” Colarusso said. “We’ve not made any concrete changes yet, but that experience has led to discussions around what tools we can leverage to create a deeper relationship with people who are coming to our site for the first time.”

Other Massachusetts-based outlets in this quarter’s data included The New Bedford Light, The Newton Beacon, the Plymouth Independent, and The Belmont Voice.

Other outlets with notable gains this quarter:

Votebeat, the national nonprofit covering U.S. elections, saw a 154% increase in website visits in July, up from 62,600 visits in June. Growth and community editor Lauren Aguirre said that jump was the result of publishing a scoop that President Trump had fired all of the members of the Election Assistance Commission.

That story alone brought in 110,047 pageviews, and 17% of those came from Reddit.

“With the demise of Twitter, we’ve really been leaning into Reddit and other spaces where political nerds like to hang out,” Aguirre said. “The outsized attention this story received on Reddit is absolutely due to our continued presence over there. Before Votebeat began posting on Reddit a few years ago, we’d almost never be linked in communities like this.”

Shelterforce, a nonprofit publication covering affordable housing, saw its July traffic increase by 85%, from 43,100 in June to 79,800. Director of editorial operations Lillian Ortiz attributed the spike to a story about a federal government proposal that put rental assistance at risk. That story received 18,000 pageviews and is one of the site’s top stories of the year. Ortiz also suspects that more readers are becoming listeners as Shelterforce grows its offering of audio versions of its stories. So far this year, Shelterforce has logged 30,000 listens, a 16% increase over 2025.

“Many of our authors read their stories, and that has helped us reach new audiences and give people another way to engage with our work,” Ortiz said. “While the audio is embedded with stories on our website, people can also listen to us on other audio-streaming platforms. We also offer AI-generated audio for stories that aren’t read by a person.”

The Buckeye Flame, which covers LGBTQ+ issues in Ohio, got 45,000 unique visits in July, up from 25,000 in June. Editor Ken Schneck said that the Flame continued to report on its usual beats, including state politics and rural issues, and no particular story drove a surge in traffic.

“The July traffic is so affirming because we literally changed nothing about how we do what we do,” Schneck said. “Our goal is to publish a new piece every weekday and to amplify topics ranging from policy and legislation to rural coverage to queer joy, and that’s exactly what happened for us in July.”

The Imprint, a national nonprofit covering the child welfare and juvenile justice systems, saw an 82% increase in its August traffic over July, from 68,500 to 124,800. Co-executive director Christie Renick said one story — about the state of Utah revoking the license of a mental health treatment facility following complaints from advocates including Paris Hilton — drove much of that traffic and resulted in nearly 25,000 pageviews. (Renick couldn’t find any evidence that Hilton herself shared the story.)

The Juneau Independent saw a 40% increase in visits from July to August, and a 31% increase from August to September. In real numbers, the Independent went from 41,800 visits in July to 77,300 by the end of September.

The news of the spike was a surprise to editor Mark Sabbatini, who makes up one-fourth of the newsroom that launched in June 2025 to cover Alaska’s capital. Sabbatini attributed the August traffic growth to the Independent’s coverage of a glacial lake outburst flood, “a disaster-level event Juneau has experienced every August for the past four years.”

“We see it as a core responsibility to provide the best possible coverage before, during and after those floods, and our staff worked around the clock to provide updates as flooding peaked and during its aftermath. In addition to high local readership, that coverage is also read, cited, and republished elsewhere,” Sabbatini said. “It seems fair to state the Independent and [public radio station] KTOO are now considered Juneau’s primary news sources and what people were relying on for critical information as an emergency situation unfolded.”

And whether you choose to work primarily from home or collaborate in-person from one of our offices in Columbus, Austin, the Bay Area, or New York City, you’ll have the support to work in the way that works best for you.

Microsoft Advertising is rolling out rebuilt automated bidding models. Learn what is changing for Target CPA and Target ROAS campaigns and what to review now.

Microsoft Advertising is rolling out what it calls its biggest bidding model upgrade in a decade. The new models use more signals to predict whether an ad click will turn into a conversion and what it might be worth.

Microsoft will apply the upgrade automatically as it reaches more accounts. That means campaigns can start spending differently before you make any changes yourself. Microsoft announced the rollout on November 18 and plans more bidding updates in 2027.

Microsoft says the new models can change how quickly campaigns spend and how closely they stick to your targets. These are the areas to keep an eye on:

A $50 CPA target still leaves room for a campaign to bring in conversions at $40 each, even if it spends its full budget. A max CPC can limit that flexibility. Say you average $3 a click and cap bids at $5. The cap rules out a $6 bid even if Microsoft expects the click could bring in a conversion within your CPA target.

Say you raise your CPA target on Monday and customers usually take a week to buy. By Friday, you know what Monday’s clicks cost, but you may still be waiting on some of the sales. Faster bidding won’t shorten the time those customers take to buy.

Raising a CPA target or lowering a ROAS target can open up auctions your campaign previously passed up. To limit swings in performance, Microsoft suggests making those changes in 15% increments and reviewing each after one conversion cycle. For a bigger change, like switching bid strategies or adding a conversion goal, Microsoft recommends allowing one to two cycles.

Microsoft recommends conversion-based bidding for new campaigns once the account has at least five conversions. Those can come from campaigns you already run. If you’re still gathering your first five, Enhanced CPC is an option.

On LinkedIn, Sophie Westall asked if the same advice applies to low-volume accounts already using Enhanced CPC. Microsoft Advertising Liaison Navah Hopkins replied:

Every account is different so a blanket recommendation still needs to be put to the test. With that said, so long as the account has at least 5 conversions total, the system is smart enough to use that to begin with conversion-based bidding. While we still recommend the 30-day evaluation period and not making too many changes if you’re working with fewer conversions, the system is much more responsive now!

For judging performance, Microsoft recommends around 30 conversions in 30 days at the campaign or portfolio level. A low-volume campaign can reach the end of that first month and still have too few conversions to judge the switch.

Microsoft reported 10% more conversion value per click at roughly the same ROAS after the model upgrade. That result came from August 2026 global Search and Audience Network data for advertisers using Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS.

Microsoft also looked at advertisers who switched bid strategies. Search advertisers who moved from Target CPA to Target ROAS saw 8% more conversion value at a similar ROAS. Advertisers who moved from Enhanced CPC to Maximize Conversions with a CPA target saw 18% more conversions at a similar CPA.

If you’re considering Target ROAS, pull up a few recent purchases in Microsoft Advertising and compare the reported values with the order totals. A $40 order and a $400 order can both show up as conversions even if your tracking assigns them the same value. That’s easy to miss if you’re used to checking that purchases are coming through and leaving it there.

Microsoft reported its largest gains from value-based bidding among advertisers who sent actual transaction values. If your purchase goal uses a fixed value, the reported ROAS reflects that estimate. It can move as you sell more or spend less, but it won’t capture a change in how much customers spend per order.

With lead gen, you may need time to get a better read on what a conversion is worth. Two people can submit the same form, and sales may find out a week later that only one is a fit.

Pedro Bailaderia asked Navah Hopkins about sending an estimate at submission and updating it once more information comes into the CRM. Hopkins supported using the Conversions API or offline imports. She also advised setting a ROAS target that reflects the values you send.

If your team is still working out how to value a qualified lead, that’s worth settling before you set a ROAS target. A campaign can hit the target you set while sales is still waiting for more leads it can work with.

If a campaign already brings in the sales or leads you need at a cost you’re happy with, you can give the upgrade some room before changing anything. Keeping your settings steady makes it easier to see how the new models work with the goals and budget you already have.

The rollout may be more useful if you’ve been adjusting targets to get a campaign to spend more evenly. If delivery settles down on its own, you may have fewer reasons to touch those targets during the week. That would leave you freer to change them when the business needs more volume or can afford to pay more for a conversion.

Our apps, Raya and Places, are tools for discovery of and access to exciting people and places globally. We believe that by marrying great software with a membership-based community built around core values of trust, curation, and authenticity, we can provide solutions that offer something different to infinite content and AI-slop. Places’ mission is to help discerning global travelers find their favorite places wherever they go through expert curation and community trust.

As a Data Scientist on the Places by Raya team you will play a key role that will shape how the Places app uses data to drive business decisions. This hands-on role combines data modeling and reporting with product analysis and experimentation. While the product itself has existed since 2023 the culture is very much like a new start-up with leadership being heavily invested in this product space and this role being the first dedicated Data Scientist to this space and supported by a dedicated Data Engineer.

We are seeking an entrepreneurial and driven data scientist to identify opportunities to improve retention and help the team evaluate and act on them. This will be a fun role for someone who wants to build data solutions from the ground up and help shape how the entire team uses insights. This person should be able to articulate best practices, develop new analytical frameworks that tie user actions to outcomes, and strike the right balance between analytical rigor and pragmatic business action.

Successful candidates will demonstrate technical skills, product expertise, and business acumen, and be enthusiastic about making a positive impact through timely execution. You are passionate about leveraging the power of data to drive product changes with quality and agility and can demonstrate sound judgment under uncertainty.

#7368. “A healthy degree of vitality”: Medill takes a look at the Twin Cities’ local news ecosystem

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

RELATED ARTICLEThe New York Times will launch a local newsletter pilot in the Twin Cities next monthSophie CulpepperJuly 9, 2026This year’s State of Local News Report from Medill was grim. But in the Twin Cities, Neal St. Anthony writes, a rich local news ecosystem offers a more hopeful picture. The metro area of more than 3 million people is home to The Minnesota Star Tribune, public radio powerhouse MPR, local TV stations, and multiple successful nonprofit startups, from nearly two-decade-old MinnPost to Sahan Journal (whose founder, Mukhtar Ibrahim, also launched The Somali Brief this fall). Axios has published an Axios Local newsletter for the Twin Cities since 2021, and this summer, The New York Times launched its own Twin Cities local newsletter.

RELATED ARTICLEWith Washington Post Local diminished, other news sites step up their D.C. coverageSophie CulpepperMarch 5, 2026The question this ecosystem raises, according to St. Anthony, is “whether the Twin Cities represents the potential future of local news in metros across the country: a robust ecosystem with no dominant mass-market player but more news outlets tailored to smaller, niche audiences with narrower but deep interests.” (That description brings to mind other urban media markets where a diffuse ecosystem of smaller, newer players have stepped up as legacy media pulls back.)

“There is a healthy degree of vitality in local news in the Twin Cities. The story elsewhere is ‘news deserts’ and little original journalism,” University of Minnesota professor Benjamin Toff told St. Anthony. While local institutions like the Star Tribune have survived, he added, “it’s not immune to industry forces, including the veritable disappearance of print.”

A few highlights from St. Anthony’s piece for Medill:

On MPR: After the 2025 rescission of federal funding for public media, Minnesota Public Radio lost about $6 million. But MPR, like other public broadcasters, was able to turn the rescission into a highly successful fundraising campaign. Its 2026 fiscal revenue rose 5% to $119 million, and it grew to 172,000 paying members, a record.

#7367. Snapchat will show more info on mutual friends

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The app will allow users who opt in to see a list of friends they have in common with someone, directly on their profile.

Snapchat wants to get more people talking in the app, so it’s expanding its info display on mutual friends. The updated format will enable users to see expanded profile info for any friends that they have in common with connections.

As shown in these example screens, Snapchat’s mutual friends update will give users more info about friends they have in common directly on their profile display.

To be clear, Snapchat already displays a count of how many friends users have in common. The mutual friends feature builds on that by showing who those friends are.

That could get more people interacting, and given the slowdown of Snapchat’s audience growth, that could be a critical focus.

Snapchat’s user growth has been stagnating, especially in the U.S. and Europe, where its daily active user count has been flat through the third quarter. As such, Snapchat needs to capitalize on its existing audience in order to maximize opportunities and drive advertiser interest.

Maybe offering more specific connection tools could help boost audience interest.

The question then is whether Snapchat users will actually want to display their expanded information to friends of friends, or whether they’d prefer to keep their Snapchat friend circles exclusive.

Given the more private focus of the app, the latter seems more likely, but again, Snapchat needs to try new things in order to drive user activity.

Snapchat also said that both the user and their connections will have to opt-in to the feature before their expanded information is displayed to others.

Mutual friends is now available to Snapchat users in the U.S., Australia, France and Sweden on iOS and Android.

#7366. After gutting newsrooms, McClatchy plans to rebuild itself around AI

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.

Two months after McClatchy Media laid off more than 90 journalists nationwide, executives at the storied local newspaper chain offered a blunt assessment of its future.

The award-winning local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company was no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month, and its survival depended on a wholesale reinvention — centered entirely around artificial intelligence.

From the rollout of new lifestyle websites that feature AI-generated articles and sponsored content to legal review and finance, executives revealed how AI is now integrated into virtually every part of the company. The demonstration comes after McClatchy, one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates, carried out deep staff cuts in September at the Miami Herald, The Kansas City Star, and more than a dozen other local news outlets. An anonymous “person close to the executive decision-making” told The New York Times the layoffs were not about AI and were instead about “business performance in some areas.”

A companywide blueprint presented during the meeting highlights how McClatchy is systematically outsourcing the infrastructure for local news to AI agents — and rebranding around lifestyle verticals for sports fans, outdoor enthusiasts, and true-crime junkies.

Dubbed “Project Catalyst,” the companywide restructure will create an “AI-native operating model” that takes “repeated tasks off of humans” and embeds AI agents “directly into the daily workflow,” Jeff Dorsey, McClatchy’s chief operating officer, said at the town hall. Dorsey described the initiative as an effort to automate “non-core as well as core functions,” “get rid of things that just don’t offer the same value” they once did, and “provide cash, frankly, to keep the business afloat.”

McClatchy, which operates 29 daily newspapers across 14 states, didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment.

Central to the rebrand is the launch of four new websites: Crime Hunter, a site devoted to “real-life crime and justice”; Saltwater South, which “celebrates the places, people and experiences that make the coastal South unlike anywhere else”; Camp & Country, a “national outdoor destination”; and Student Section, billed as “the home of the college sports fan.”

Each of the sites is “powered by Trend Hunter,” a company McClatchy acquired in 2024 that uses AI “to glean insights into consumer trends” and sell consumer goods like $33.91 rosemary oil “to support a healthy scalp environment,” a $249 red light therapy cap to regrow hair “without the hassle of messy serums” and $34.99 “MAGIC Mushroom Coffee” for “clarity, balance and natural energy.”

Little discussed, however, were the company’s local news ambitions. Kristine Sherred, chair of the Washington State NewsGuild and the food and dining reporter at The News Tribune in Tacoma, Washington, said that she and other journalists were left to wonder “why we were even invited.”

“Our takeaway was that it wasn’t about news,” Sherred said. “The future McClatchy appears to be building does not seem aligned with the mission of journalism.”

The meeting this month offered the clearest roadmap to date about McClatchy’s all-in approach to AI as one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates navigates traffic declines, shifting consumer habits, and heavy debt obligations. It also comes at a critical moment for a media industry that seeks to modernize with AI — technology simultaneously blamed for gutting web traffic and touted as a tool to cut costs.

“There is no sector that has not been disrupted this year by AI — everyone is going through extraordinary disruption,” Hunter said. Through a laser focus on AI-powered efficiencies, he said, the company can turn around its fortunes. “We can win — not with yesterday’s solutions, though.”

For McClatchy, which has undergone aggressive cost-cutting efforts since it was acquired by New Jersey-based hedge fund Chatham Asset Management in 2020, its pivot toward AI-generated content over the last year has been met with internal pushback and, from some readers, ridicule.

In May, journalists at The Sacramento Bee, the Miami Herald, and other McClatchy-owned papers withheld their names from articles that were produced with its “content scaling agent,” a chatbot that repackages human-written news articles at varying lengths for different audiences — complete with reporters’ names.

Similar resistance has played out at other news outlets. Earlier this month, for example, reporters at the Akron Beacon Journal in Ohio withheld their bylines for two weeks to protest a tool that generates AI summaries of articles that, the journalists allege, undermines their work and provides readers false information.

Many news organizations prohibit the publication of AI-generated articles. But for McClatchy, they’ve become a core part of its business strategy and, according to Hunter, a key part of its “company-wide effort to agentify the entire enterprise.” During a contentious virtual meeting in May, Hunter pleaded with skeptical journalists to get on board or find another job.

Anyone at McClatchy can now build AI tools to support their workflows, Rajiv Pant, McClatchy’s chief product and engineering officer, said earlier this month.

“In every one of these, humans are at the command center, they aren’t just checking the technology’s work,” Pant said. “They set the direction, make the calls and own the results. The technology lets each one of them do more of the work that only they can do.”

Trend Hunter content — including AI-generated posts — now appears regularly across McClatchy’s local publications and social media feeds, including articles with little connection to the communities those outlets have historically served. Recent examples include a post about winter “barn jackets” in the Miami Herald and a feature about collegiate football in Texas for the Kansas City Star.

Other posts highlight obscure beauty products and questionable health trends, including how nugget ice “has become the craze worth understanding,” how saunas have “reshaped social wellness,” and “what your poop color, shape and frequency say about your gut health.”

Or, as one Kansas City Star reporter put it, the layoffs have created news websites where it’s “city reporters out, shitty reporters in.”

“They’re trying to kind of go toward these buzzy-type topics instead of local journalism that holds people to account,” said the reporter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to retaliation concerns.

Readers, an overwhelming majority of whom are skeptical of AI use in newsrooms, have also taken notice. In a post on X, one social media user wrote that “people want the news” not “AI generated slop.” Another called into question McClatchy’s decision to publish an article — across numerous local news brands — about why the actress Scarlett Johansson “changed her magnesium supplement routine after a spray left her feet feeling dry.”

This AI slop is what McClatchy forced a bunch of its newspapers to publish in unison a few weeks ago. Who needs real human reporters when you can have this? https://t.co/Z82Vg67WtH

— James (@jameslineky) September 10, 2026

Given the rapid spread of AI-generated content online, McClatchy executives see the brand credibility of its legacy publications as a differentiator. Over time, Hunter said, the market will reward trust — and McClatchy is well positioned to capitalize on its local news audiences.

“It is important that we have credible, accurate and relevant content,” Hunter said. “We are not running from our standards, but we’re running toward a new model to help customers make better decisions.”

In recent months, as much as 20% of articles published by McClatchy newspapers were AI-generated, according to data from AI-detection company Originality.ai. (AI detection tools like Originality are imprecise in distinguishing synthetic writing from human-authored content.) Rather than building new audiences, McClatchy’s use of AI-generated content could erode trust among readers, said Jon Gillham, Originality’s founder and CEO.

Such a reality is already playing out in Washington, said Sherred of the Washington State NewsGuild. Sherred’s union went on strike in May to demand “ethical limits” around the company’s use of AI. The guild said in a statement at the time it was negotiating for “freedom to write hard-hitting news stories that take time, and not be punished if we don’t churn out clickbait.”

“We hear this from people in the community all the time: They don’t want short snippets, they don’t want rehashed work and they don’t want AI telling them the news,” Sherred said. “The only way you get high-quality local news is by having high-quality local reporters actually out there making it.”

Less than a week after McClatchy laid off journalists nationwide in September, executives sent the remaining staff an emoji-laced email announcing “fresh talent”: several executives, two reporters and three editors for its “Content Innovation Lab” — the engine behind its new AI-powered lifestyle verticals.

A recent job listing for innovation lab writers notes the “company’s future depends” on an embrace of AI and the innovation lab is its “next-generation approach to content” where emerging technologies are leveraged to “fuel experimentation and productivity.”

“From barbecue to bourbon, water sports to hiking, and golf to college sports, we are going to develop a steady stream of reader-focused, high-quality content for national and regional audiences,” according to the job listing. Producers will use AI to launch new brands “tied to dedicated communities of interest around travel, food, outdoor recreation, sports and even crime.”

The insights into the company’s future editorial direction come on the heels of its steepest staff reduction in years, with layoffs of investigative reporters, government watchdogs, and other journalists focused on local news.

“The city of Tacoma no longer has a city reporter,” Sherred said. “What’s the purpose of a local paper if you have no one covering your local government?”

Hired to lead the Content Innovation Lab is Patrick Stiegman, a 20-year ESPN digital veteran who, during the meeting this month, turned to sports media lingo to describe the goal behind Saltwater South, Camp & Country, and its other AI-powered lifestyle brands. By “cultivating passionate fans” around obsessive lifestyle niches, he said, the company seeks to leverage reader data “and monetization opportunities” to guide coverage decisions.

Perhaps nobody put McClatchy’s pivot in starker terms than Ariel Storch, recently hired to lead an AI-powered rebrand of its video strategy.

“We make entertainment — not content, entertainment,” Storch said during the Nov. 6 meeting. “Think about a late-night show. Nobody tunes in to be informed, they tune in to laugh. The by-product is you leave knowing about a new movie, a new book, a new product.”

Building new audiences is critical as the company works to claw itself out of debt, said Joe Settineri, McClatchy’s chief financial officer. Stabilizing McClatchy’s core business is necessary, he said, for the Content Innovation Lab and its other AI initiatives to be successful.

“Today, most of that profitability is already spoken for because, like most companies, we have a sizable amount of debt,” Settineri said. “Like a loan on a house, we have to pay it down or you lose the house.”

#7365. Software Engineer - AI Tooling Infrastructure at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

We’re looking for a Software Engineer, AI Tooling Infrastructure to join our AI Tooling team and help build and run the backend services behind Supabase’s AI products. The Supabase MCP server is one example of what the team runs in production, alongside the services that support agent skills and the dashboard assistant. You’ll work closely with the Platform, SRE, Auth, Billing and Edge Functions teams, and with the engineers on the AI Tooling team who build the product surfaces.

The AI Tooling team runs its own services in production and carries its own on-call. Traffic from AI clients and agents behaves differently from traffic from people: hundreds of calls a minute, retry loops, and no reading of deprecation warnings. This role makes sure the services they use are reliable, correctly authorized and observable. It is a systems and infrastructure role rather than a product AI role, and it is not an SRE role. You will build and operate these systems, not only advise on them.

This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments, owns what they ship in production, and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

Build and operate the production backend services behind Supabase’s AI products, including the MCP server: deployment, scaling, configuration and release.

Take ownership of how those services are structured, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

Define, measure and meet reliability targets for the services the team runs. Set SLOs with the SRE team, track error budgets, and use them to decide what to fix first.

Participate in the AI Tooling team on-call rotation, and be a first responder for incidents in those services. Investigate, fix, coordinate with other teams during incidents, and write the follow-ups and runbooks.

Work the AI Tooling team support queue alongside on-call, and turn recurring issues into fixes rather than repeated manual answers.

Own authentication and authorization for AI and agent clients: OAuth apps, scoped tokens, and permissions that make sense for agents as well as humans, including how we change or deprecate a permission without breaking existing integrations.

Own observability for the services the team runs: metrics, traces, logs, dashboards and alerts, so we find problems before customers do.

Handle capacity and abuse for agent traffic: rate limits, cost and safety controls, and behavior under load or when a dependency degrades.

Improve the architecture of the services the team owns as they grow, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

Work with the Platform team on shared code, review ownership and release process, and with the SRE team on infrastructure, alerting and incident practice.

Contribute to the code of the AI Tooling team’s tools, such as the MCP server, where it affects reliability and security, in partnership with the engineers who own the product surface.

Have 5+ years of experience building and running backend services in production, and have carried on-call for them.

Write strong TypeScript or Go, and are comfortable working in the other.

Have designed and operated APIs with real consumers: versioning, error handling, rate limiting, and backwards-compatible change.

Know OAuth, OIDC, JWT and API authorization well enough to debug them in production and to explain where implementations commonly deviate from the spec.

Have a good understanding of PostgreSQL and relational databases.

Are comfortable with CI/CD, Docker and containerized deployments, and with infrastructure as code. Any tool is fine.

Can debug across services: follow a slow or failing request through several systems using metrics, traces and logs.

Communicate clearly in writing, work with a wide range of stakeholders, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving quickly.

Pick your centre of gravity. We expect you to be deep in at least one of these, and to tell us which:

APIs and auth: You have designed permission models, token scopes or OAuth flows for third-party or machine clients, and you have migrated them without breaking users.

Operations: You have run production services yourself: carried the pager, written alerts and runbooks, used SLOs or similar to decide what to fix, and made shared systems less risky over time.

Gateways and distributed systems: You have built or run proxies or gateways, or debugged hard failures across services (retries, partial failures, upstream outages, fail-open vs fail-closed decisions), and you can reason about load and degradation.

Experience with agent tooling (MCP or similar), or serving traffic from AI agents and LLM clients.

Experience moving a service out of a larger codebase while keeping existing clients working.

Experience with Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Logflare or a similar observability stack, and real SLO work.

Open-source contributions, especially to Node.js, Go, TypeScript or API tooling.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

New remote jobs delivered to your inbox, every week.

Location independence is the future of work. It serves companies with best talent from around the globe. And benefits employees with a greater work life balance and the ability to work in their pyjamas.- Nithur, founder.

#7363. Robots.txt Guide – Best Practices For Search & AI Crawlers via @sejournal, @vahandev

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Learn how to use your robots.txt to fix crawl and indexing mistakes, and manage AI training bots, search crawlers, and user-requested website visits.

The robots.txt file has always been an essential tool for managing crawler access to a website. With AI search tools and agents now visiting websites alongside traditional crawlers, you need to know which rules each one follows.

But, blocking the wrong bot can exclude your content from LLMs or SERPs, while leaving unnecessary URLs open can waste crawl budget on large sites. So, you need to know what you are doing.

This guide will help you understand how robots.txt rules work so you can avoid common robots.txt mistakes, keep useful content accessible, but at the same time limit unnecessary crawling.

The robots.txt is a simple text file that sits in the root directory of your site and tells crawlers what should be crawled.

The table below provides a quick reference to the key robots.txt directives.

This 2024 screenshot shows an example of robots.txt from ikea.com with multiple rules.

Note that robots.txt doesn’t support full regular expressions and only has two wildcards:

Also, note that URL path matching is case-sensitive, e.g., “filter=” is not equal to “Filter=.” The directive names and user-agent matching are case-insensitive.

When setting up a robots.txt file, it’s important to know the order in which search engines decide which rules to apply in case of conflicting rules.

When you write a separate set of rules for a bot, it follows those rules instead of the rules under User-agent: *. For example:

Here, Googlebot can crawl /private/ because its own rules allow every URL to be crawled. To block that directory for Googlebot, add Disallow: /private/ beneath its Allow: / line.

Within the applicable group, Google follows these two key rules:

The rule that matches more characters in the URL will be applied. For example:

In this case, the “Allow: /downloads/free/” rule is more specific than “Disallow: /downloads/” because it targets a subdirectory.

Google will allow crawling of subfolder “/downloads/free/” but block everything else under “/downloads/.”

When multiple rules are equally specific, for example:

Google will choose the least restrictive one. This means Google will allow access to /downloads/.

Google’s 2024 reminder about action URLs focused on add-to-cart and wishlist links that waste crawler and server resources.

Imagine you have an online store with hundreds of thousands of pages. There are sections of websites like filtered pages that may have an infinite number of versions. Those pages don’t have unique value, essentially contain duplicate content, and may create infinite crawl space, thus wasting your server and Googlebot’s resources. That is where robots.txt comes in, preventing search engine bots from crawling those pages.

If you don’t do that, Google may try to crawl an infinite number of URLs with different (even non-existent) search parameter values, causing spikes and a waste of crawl budget.

As a general rule, you should always ask why certain pages exist, and whether they have any value for search engines to crawl and index.

Depending on your site and indexing goals, candidates for crawl restrictions include:

Let’s dive into examples of how you can use robots.txt for each case.

Internal search results are a common source of unnecessary crawling by Google and other search engines. If those results are not intended to appear in search, consider restricting their crawl space.

On WordPress websites, it is usually an “s” parameter, and the URL looks like this:

Gary Illyes from Google has repeatedly warned to block “action” URLs as they can cause Googlebot to crawl them indefinitely even non-existent URLs with different combinations.

Here is the rule you can use in your robots.txt to block such URLs from being crawled:

This crawl-stats screenshot, included in the original 2024 guide, illustrates reduced crawling of non-existent internal search URLs after they were blocked via robots.txt.

Note that Google may index blocked pages based on links to their URLs. Robots.txt does not guarantee their removal from search. If removal is your goal, use noindex and allow Google to crawl the page so it can read that instruction.

Faceted navigation is an integral part of every ecommerce website. There can be cases where faceted navigation is part of an SEO strategy and aimed at ranking for general product searches.

Zalando’s color-based landing pages, such as those targeting “gray t-shirt” illustrate this approach. The principle is to keep useful search landing pages crawlable while restricting unwanted filter combinations.

However, in most cases, this is not the case, and filter parameters are used merely for filtering products, creating dozens of pages with duplicate content.

There may be multiple filter parameters in one URL. Identify which ones generate unwanted crawl space; do not block facets that form part of your search strategy. Google’s faceted-navigation guidance distinguishes these two cases.

For example, if you have filters with the following parameters “sortby,” “color,” and “price,” you may use this set of rules:

These pairs match each parameter in the first position or after another parameter. Add only the parameters you intend to restrict, and test both wanted and unwanted URLs.

UTM parameters are used for tracking purposes.

In the Reddit exchange shown below, John Mueller addressed tracking parameters on external links. Keep that context separate from internally generated filter or search URLs.

Keep internal links pointed at the URLs you want crawled. Decide whether to block a parameter by what it does on your site; the presence of a query string alone is not a reason to disallow a page.

Let’s say you have a lot of PDF documents, such as product guides, brochures, or downloadable papers, and you don’t want them crawled.

Here is a simple robots.txt rule that will block search engine bots from accessing those documents:

The “Disallow: /*.pdf$” line tells crawlers not to crawl any URLs that end with .pdf.

By using /*, the rule matches any path on the website. As a result, any URL ending with .pdf will be blocked from crawling. It will not match /guide.pdf?download=1 or an uppercase .PDF extension; test any such variants separately. If you want a PDF excluded from search, use an X-Robots-Tag: noindex HTTP header and keep it crawlable so Google can read the header.

If you have a WordPress website and want to disallow PDFs from the uploads directory where you upload them via the CMS, you can use the following rule:

You can see that we have conflicting rules here.

In case of conflicting rules, the more specific one takes priority, which means the last line ensures that only the specific file located in folder “wp-content/uploads/2024/09/allowed-document.pdf” is allowed to be crawled.

Let’s say you have an API endpoint where you submit your data from the form. It is likely your form has an action attribute like action=”/form/submissions/.”

If a crawler discovers the URL /form/submissions/, you may want to prevent crawling of that path. You can request that with this rule:

By specifying a directory in the Disallow rule, you are telling the crawlers to avoid crawling all pages under that directory, and you don’t need to use the (*) wildcard anymore, like “/form/*.”

Note that you must always specify relative paths and never absolute URLs, like “https://www.example.com/form/” for Disallow and Allow directives.

Be cautious to avoid malformed rules. For example, using /form without a trailing slash will also match a page /form-design-examples/, which may be a page on your blog that you want to index.

Read: 8 Common Robots.txt Issues And How To Fix Them

If you have an ecommerce website, you likely have directories that start with “/myaccount/,” such as “/myaccount/orders/” or “/myaccount/profile/.”

With the top page “/myaccount/” being a sign-in page that you want to be indexed and found by users in search, you may want to disallow the subpages from being crawled by Googlebot.

You can use the Disallow rule in combination with the Allow rule to block everything under the “/myaccount/” directory (except the /myaccount/ page).

And again, since Google uses the most specific rule, it will disallow everything under the /myaccount/ directory but allow only the /myaccount/ page to be crawled.

Here’s another use case of combining the Disallow and Allow rules: in case you have your search under the /search/ directory and want it to be found and indexed but block actual search URLs:

Every website uses JavaScript, and many of these scripts are not related to the rendering of content, such as tracking scripts or those used for loading AdSense.

Only block a script after confirming it is unnecessary for rendering the content and links you want indexed. Use URL Inspection to check the rendered page; blocking a shared bundle or a script with rendering dependencies can prevent Google from seeing important content. A robots.txt file on your host also cannot control a script fetched from a different host.

Below is a sample line that is disallowing sample JavaScript, which contains tracking pixels.

You can block training bots while allowing AI tools to find your pages and retrieve them for users. The key is to give training, search, and user-requested AI crawlers separate rules.

Publishers may block training to limit the use of their reporting without attribution, while ecommerce brands may welcome it if product mentions lead people to search and buy. Because the benefits differ by business, developers should set these rules with stakeholders.

Disallowing training bots cannot guarantee that your content stays out of training datasets, because crawlers that ignore robots.txt can still collect it. It also does not force AI tools to visit or cite your site, as they may find the information elsewhere.

A BuzzStream study covered by SEJ in January 2026, found that 79% of the US and UK news sites examined disallowed at least one training bot, while 71% disallowed at least one retrieval or live-search bot. Because retrieval helps AI tools find and cite your pages, blocking those bots is a separate decision from opting out of training.

OpenAI uses OAI-SearchBot to surface websites in ChatGPT search answers, while ChatGPT-User handles user-requested visits. Because search and training permissions are separate, you can allow OAI-SearchBot and ChatGPT-User while blocking GPTBot.

This example blocks OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s training crawlers while allowing their search and user-requested bots, along with Perplexity’s:

In the example above, /private/ is an excluded directory. Replace it with any paths you want to keep those bots from crawling.

Most major AI crawlers follow robots.txt, including OpenAI’s GPTBot and Anthropic’s ClaudeBot.

User-requested visits work differently because some providers allow their bots to bypass robots.txt or generally ignore it when acting on a user’s request. OpenAI says robots.txt may not apply to ChatGPT-User, and Perplexity says Perplexity-User generally ignores it. Anthropic says its bots, including Claude-User, honor robots.txt. Because robots.txt only tells bots which URLs they may crawl, you need authentication to protect private content.

The bot tokens and robots.txt policies for Copilot’s browser visits, Grok, DeepSeek, and Meta Muse remain unknown because I could not verify them in the providers’ public documentation.

Google and Apple provide separate robots.txt tokens for controlling how crawled content is used:

Google-Extended covers Gemini training and specified grounding uses, where source content helps generate an answer. Blocking it does not block Googlebot or affect ordinary Google Search inclusion. Applebot-Extended controls foundation-model training without blocking Applebot’s search crawl. Neither token is a separate crawler, so these rules do not reduce crawling requests by themselves.

After changing the file, check your server log files and confirm that your firewall allows the bots you want. Use server or CDN controls when you need to enforce access restrictions.

For background, see SEJ’s earlier coverage of AI content use and AI chatbot traffic.

Including your sitemap URL in the robots.txt file helps search engines easily discover all the important pages on your website. This is done by adding a specific line that points to your sitemap location, and you can specify multiple sitemaps, each on its own line.

Unlike Allow or Disallow rules, which allow only a relative path, the Sitemap directive requires a full, absolute URL to indicate the location of the sitemap.

Ensure the sitemaps’ URLs are accessible to search engines and have proper syntax to avoid errors.

The crawl-delay directive in robots.txt specifies the number of seconds a bot should wait before crawling the next page. While Googlebot does not recognize the crawl-delay directive, other bots may respect it.

It helps prevent server overload by controlling how frequently bots crawl your site.

For example, if you want ClaudeBot to crawl your content for AI training but want to avoid server overload, you can set a crawl delay to manage the interval between requests.

This requests a 60-second delay from ClaudeBot, which Anthropic documents as supporting the non-standard Crawl-delay extension. Use this when you intend to allow that crawl. Adding a delay does not override a Disallow: / rule for the same bot; review the complete group rather than copying both policies.

Of course, there may be AI bots that don’t respect crawl delay directives. In that case, you may need to use a web firewall to rate limit them.

Once you’ve composed your robots.txt, you can use these tools to troubleshoot if the syntax is correct or if you didn’t accidentally block an important URL.

Once you’ve updated your robots.txt, you must check whether it contains any error or accidentally blocks URLs you want to be crawled, such as resources, images, or website sections.

Navigate to Settings > robots.txt to open the robots.txt report. It shows the files Google fetched and any parsing warnings or errors. You can request a recrawl after a critical change. To test whether an individual page is blocked, use URL Inspection.

The video below illustrates the report workflow; interface details may differ from the current version.

Google’s robots.txt parser is an open-source parser and matcher based on the implementation used in Google’s crawler.

It requires advanced skills to install and run on your local computer. But it is highly recommended to take time and do it as instructed on that page because you can validate your changes in the robots.txt file before uploading to your server in line with the official Google parser.

Robots.txt rules apply to the host, protocol, and port where the file is requested. If you need crawl restrictions on a subdomain, its robots.txt URL must serve the rules or redirect to a file that does; the parent domain’s file is not inherited.

It creates challenges when you have a website with a dozen subdomains, as it means you should maintain a bunch of robots.txt files separately.

However, it is possible to host a robots.txt file on a subdomain, such as https://cdn.example.com/robots.txt, and set up a redirect from https://www.example.com/robots.txt to it.

You can do vice versa and host it only under the root domain and redirect from subdomains to the root.

Google applies the retrieved rules to the host that originally requested robots.txt, not automatically to the host storing the shared file. Configure a redirect from each host you want to manage, and check that the shared paths make sense for all of them.

It helps make updates and maintenance more efficient. Otherwise, you would need to use a separate robots.txt file for each subdomain.

A properly optimized robots.txt file is crucial for managing a website’s crawl budget. It ensures that search engines like Googlebot spend their time on valuable pages rather than wasting resources on unnecessary ones.

Blocking compliant crawlers can reduce unwanted requests. For AI systems, distinguish crawl restrictions from training-use controls, and verify the effect in your logs. Google-Extended and Applebot-Extended do not stop a separate crawler.

Make sure you always validate your changes to avoid unexpected crawlability issues.

However, remember that crawl demand and serving capacity both matter. Useful content, efficient page loading, and a healthy server remain important alongside robots.txt rules.

#7360. Meta launches messaging app for teens

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company’s new Direct app is designed to expand Instagram DMs to a separate platform, and is almost exactly the same as the Direct app that the company launched in 2017.

Meta is testing a new, separate direct messaging app, which aims to expand Instagram DMs to its own platform, and could help Meta soften the impacts of expanding teen social media bans.

Called Direct, this latest app is aimed at teenagers, and offers a range of creation tools and features that align with teen usage behaviors.

As shown in these example images, Direct users draw on their chat threads, view inbox notes — a feature ported from IG — add stickers and voice effects, and more.

None of which is overly surprising, because Meta has actually launched this exact app before.

Back in 2017, Meta launched a messaging app for younger users, which was also called "Direct," and looks very similar to this new iteration.

That version of Direct was also focused on fun DM interactions, and included elements like drawing and effects in order to appeal to younger audiences.

Which obviously didn’t catch on then, so why is Meta now treading the same path, and trying, once again, to facilitate DM interaction between younger users?

Well, primarily, because Snapchat is struggling.

Snapchat’s user growth has stalled in the U.S. and Europe, with the app’s daily active user counts actually declining in both markets throughout the year.

With interest in Snapchat waning, Meta likely sees an opportunity to step in and provide an alternate platform for teen DMs.

It’s also worth noting that Meta launched an initial test of Direct in Turkey, which just this month enacted restrictions on social media usage for users under age 15.

As reported by Politico, Turkey’s social media ban for users under age 15 came into effect on Nov. 1. The law relates to all foreign-originated social media apps, but messaging apps are not included in the restrictions.

As such, Meta likely sees an opportunity to step in and scoop up any teens who may get booted from Snapchat as a result of this update.

Of course, Instagram and Facebook will also be impacted by these restrictions, and providing an alternative option for teen connection could ensure that Meta can soften any potential usage impacts. But an alternative messaging app won’t necessarily reduce the impact on its ads business, as it’s unlikely to inject ads into a DM focused app.

This is why Snapchat is likely the bigger focus, in terms of diluting its market share and increasing Meta’s own dominance.

In February, Snapchat reported that it had locked or disabled over 415,000 user accounts in Australia that the company identified as belonging to users under age 16, in line with Australia’s teen social media restrictions.

Australia’s population is around a third of Turkey’s, which points to the potential opportunity if Meta can replace Snap. Meta is also testing Direct in Thailand as well, which is also considering tougher teen social media restrictions, according to Thai PBS World.

Meta could use this as an opportunity to become the next critical platform for teen user engagement, with the scale of its other apps helping to promote its direct messaging app to users who would be impacted by these bans.

Meta also said that Direct will include a range of advanced protection measures, and will be subject to Meta’s parental supervision tools.

It’s an interesting tactic, though it will likely raise the eyebrows of local officials, who could see this as an attempt by Meta to circumvent social media restrictions. However, the logic applied to teen social media bans, in terms of content exposure, doesn’t necessarily apply to messaging apps.

And if Meta has the scale and capability to quickly scale messaging platforms faster than its competitors, it makes sense. And given that it’s already launched the exact same app once before, the broader effort here is likely worth the test.

#7358. OpenAI Publishes Prompting Guidance For GPT-6.2 Astra via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

OpenAI's GPT-6.2 guide says Astra writes more concisely by default, suggests revisiting "be concise" prompts and flags an API change for edited history.

OpenAI is suggesting that developers who are migrating to GPT-6.2 Astra should revisit instructions such as “be concise” when they update their system prompts. The guide for developers on how to use GPT-6.2 states that Astra produces output that is more direct and brief by default than prior GPT models.

The company’s guidance for GPT-6 Astra says the model tends toward detailed, formatted responses.

GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol launched Nov. 17. Developers can use both in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol.

Astra is described in the GPT-6.2 guide as “more concise and direct by default than earlier models,” with an adjustable overall tone that can range from a professional colleague to a more conversational assistant.

The GPT-6.2 guide provides an example prompt for apps that use the model as a collaborator in day-to-day work. This prompt tells Astra to stick with the terminology of the user and its sources and to address the key points at the outset of its response.

The GPT-6 guidance states, “GPT-6 Astra tends to use lists, tables and Markdown to make responses scannable.” The GPT-6 guide also contains an example prompt for apps that require prose with less formatting. This example prompt requests “clear, concise paragraphs” and directs the model to reserve lists for presenting parallel or sequential data.

The GPT-5.6 guide states that GPT-5.6 is generally more concise by default than GPT-5.5, and that brevity instructions (such as “Be concise” and “Keep it short”) may be unnecessary for some types of task.

The GPT-6.2 guide advises asking the model to adjust for its target audience in emails, documents and any other writing intended for an external reader. It does this by suggesting a prompt which states that an external audience would probably have less understanding of the user’s context, so the model will need to provide the background information that audience needs.

The prompt also provides guidance on editing by instructing the model to “preserve the author’s content and wording” when reviewing or editing existing work and adhere to the user’s direction as to what changes are to be made.

When performing longer tasks, the model can retain abbreviations, jargon or shorthand from the reasoning process, or from other agents, in its final answers. The guide suggests a method to address this by having the model write a self-contained response for anyone who hasn’t been tracking progress updates. Additionally, the guide’s example prompt tells the model not to include such shorthand, jargon or abbreviations in the response.

The guide says GPT-6.2 Astra may propose a next step and wait for confirmation when a user’s intent is unclear. For work that can run on its own, the guide’s advice is to spell out the outcome the model should complete and which decisions need the user’s input.

The guide’s suggested prompts tell the model to make reasonable, reversible assumptions and keep working, stating what it assumed. It should stop and ask only when the task’s scope changes in a big way, when it’s blocked, or when the user has to make a decision. It should also check in before irreversible or destructive actions.

The guide also points to an async question tool, which lets GPT-6.2 ask the user a question while it keeps working on anything that doesn’t depend on the answer. OpenAI’s async tool calling page says the app defines that tool and shows the question to the user, and that it isn’t a built-in tool in the Responses API.

Starting with GPT-6.2, the API will drop reasoning items as soon as it identifies that the client has made an edit to prior history, dropped down to a lower model version, or changed the end-user account or organization, according to OpenAI’s API documentation. Reasoning items provide the model’s reasoning from earlier in the conversation. Dropping these can lead to a reduction in answer quality and increase the number of tokens used by the model to repeat previous work.

Examples on OpenAI’s page about the change include shortening a tool result, rewriting a developer message (which carries an app’s instructions), and replacing older turns with a summary. For new instructions, the page suggests appending a developer message that asks the model to ignore older instructions and follow the new ones, in place of editing the original.

Teams building drafting or editing tools on GPT-6 Astra have prompts to review prior to migrating to GPT-6.2 Astra. Developers need to revisit any instruction that asks GPT-6 Astra to produce briefer answers, according to the 6.2 guide. Some of these tools may rewrite their own instructions as well during a conversation. This could lead to GPT-6.2 Astra losing its earlier reasoning, and spending additional tokens to recreate this process.

The GPT-6.2 guide calls its prompts a starting point, based on behavior seen with GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol. The GPT-6 guidance is still on the same page as the 6.2 guide, under its own tab, so teams can compare what each guide says about the model they’re moving from.

For reasoning effort, the 6.2 migration notes recommend medium for new integrations and low for apps that are currently set to none or minimal. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 guide, which I covered in September, also asked developers to retest effort settings carried over from Opus 5.

#7356. Snapchat shares insight into luxury shopping trends

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A new study commissioned by the app found that 84% of its users said social media platforms made them feel close to the luxury universe.

Snapchat has published a new report which examines key trends among luxury shoppers, as well as the role that Snapchat itself plays in connecting shoppers to new luxury products.

The report is based on a survey of more than 9,000 luxury consumers across nine global markets, which was conducted by APP Media and Ifop group.

The data underlines the role that social media plays in raising awareness of luxury products, and specifically highlights Snapchat’s role in helping to inform and validate luxury shopping decisions.

The data shows that 76% of luxury shoppers agreed that social platforms make them feel close to the luxury universe. Snapchat users are even more aligned with this, with 84% of them agreeing with the statement.

The report also looked at how luxury shoppers approach buying, including their motivations for shopping for higher-end products.

The report also includes a range of helpful data points for marketing plans, such as info on the impact of scarcity.

In addition, the report also explored the role that peer validation plays in the luxury goods purchase process.

The latter is an important note for Snapchat specifically, because users in the app generally engaged with smaller groups of close friends within their message streams.

Indeed, the survey data showed that content from close connections is the key driver of luxury purchase decisions for Snapchatters.

The report also included notes on the kinds of content luxury shoppers respond to, which could help to guide strategic marketing approaches.

These are some interesting and potentially valuable notes for luxury brands, offering specific insights into how social platforms, and Snapchat specifically, can help to amplify messaging and drive purchase intent.

#7351. LinkedIn adds ninth in-stream game

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The math-based puzzle, called Sumbreak, is part of the platform’s push to increase user retention and engagement.

LinkedIn has launched its ninth in-app game, with a new math-based game called Sumbreak..

As shown in these images, Sumbreak gets players to use math in order to merge numbered tiles and eventually get to a single tile.

As explained by LinkedIn Head of Games Helen Smith: “Each time you merge matching numbers on the grid, they add together, bringing you one step closer to clearing the board. The challenge is figuring out how to combine the numbers so you're left with a single final tile.”

LinkedIn members will be able to challenge others to Sumbreak, offering another means to prompt friendly rivalry in the app and drive more engagement using games instead of relying on professional connections.

In June, when the platform launched its eighth puzzle game, called Wend, Smith said that billions of puzzles had been solved in the app since games were first added in-stream in May 2024.

LinkedIn hasn’t shared specific numbers on how many of its users are playing its puzzle games, but in March 2025, the platform reported that “millions of professionals” were playing its in-stream games each day, and that 84% of users who play a game return to try again the next day.

The idea is that these in-stream games will increase user retention and engagement and improve LinkedIn’s usage stats while also driving more opportunities for conversation and connection.

On another front, LinkedIn added favorites to gaming leaderboards, making it easier to compare performance against chosen connections and rivals.

LinkedIn also added bonus puzzles to reward players who return every day, and made its games easier to find in its updated UI.

#7349. Snapchat enables Lens creation via third-party AI tools

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The new Easy Lens command line interface enables users to build Lenses using their chatbot of choice.

Snapchat is looking to help creators use their favorite AI chatbots and tools to create Lens effects for the app, with the launch of its new Easy Lens CLI, which provides a simplified connective process to link third-party AI tools into its Lens Studio system.

As shown in this image, Snapchat’s Easy Lens CLI provides a connector to help creators build Lenses via conversational prompts using the AI chatbot of their choice.

Creators can tap on the CLI option on the EasyLens website, which will provide them with instructions on how to guide their chosen AI chatbot towards Snap’s Lens creation parameters.

From there, creators can instruct the chatbot to make whatever Lens they like, and the system will convert those ideas into relevant instructions and code.

The system expands on Snapchat’s existing Easy Lens process, which makes it easier for anyone to create a Lens effect using AI prompts. This new expansion will essentially bring that same functionality to external AI chatbots, utilizing their processing capacity to build Lens features.

As explained by Snapchat: “Easy Lens already makes it simple to create a Lens from a single prompt on web and mobile. Easy Lens CLI brings that same creation flow into the tools developers use every day, so their AI assistant can take on the technical work while they focus on the creative vision.”

Snapchat said the process will enable creators to build everything “from Web Lens games with leaderboards to camera Lenses and beauty effects.”

“Their AI assistants can generate assets, build and test each Lens, fix errors along the way and send new versions to their phone in minutes,” Snapchat said. “That means a full game can go from an idea to a published Lens in a single day, without writing any code.”

The company added that all lenses created through this process will go through the same content checks as any other Snap Lens.

CLI-created Lenses will also be eligible for monetization for enrolled creators under Snapchat’s Lens+ payout scheme. Snapchat said it awarded $1.8 million in payouts to Lens+ community creators last month.

Easy Lens CLI will run on Mac, Windows and Linux, and is also available as a plugin for Claude and Codex.

#7347. How CeraVe’s ‘Dune’ deal takes the brand’s social-first playbook global

The L’Oréal brand’s first film partnership makes it the “Official Moisturizer of Arrakis” ahead of the blockbuster’s Dec. 18 release.

CeraVe last week partnered with “Dune: Part Three” to become the “Official Moisturizer of Arrakis,” the desert planet that serves as the sci-fi epic’s titular setting. The tie-up with Warner Bros. Pictures and Legendary Pictures represents the L'Oréal brand’s first film partnership, with a campaign that will roll out ahead of the movie’s Dec. 18 theatrical release.

The brand on Monday revealed the next chapter in the campaign. A humorous “Sandworm Wrangler” video, shot in the style of behind-the-scenes content, shows how a wrangler of one of the film’s iconic sandworms uses CeraVe Moisturizing Cream — which now offers 120 hours of hydration — on the dry-skinned creature.

The debut “Precious Resource” spot reimagined the lore of Arrakis, an arid planet where every drop of moisture is preserved, replacing the story’s central resource, spice, with CeraVe. The “Dune” partnership is the latest iteration of a “medutainment” strategy that combines science with entertainment and has helped grow CeraVe into a $2 billion brand.

“When it comes to the playbook, that's something we are reproducing here with ‘Dune,’” said Vincent Chauvière, global brand president at CeraVe. “It's a multipoint campaign that is social-first, starting with a bit of excitement and surprise, and then we are going full media.”

Along with co-branded content, the campaign spans paid, earned, social, digital, retail, creator and experiential activations. The brand will also launch out-of-home ads, creator gifting and corporate screening experiences, as well as sponsor film premiere events in Los Angeles and the U.K.

“Our goal is to create partnerships that extend the worlds of our films in ways that feel unexpected, culturally relevant and genuinely entertaining,” Julie Moore, executive vice president, global brand partnerships at Warner Bros. Pictures, said in a statement.

The “Dune” campaign was created and produced by OBB Bolded, OBB’s branded content studio, with content filmed in Samalayuca Dunes in Mexico and Mexico City and directed by Maca Rubio from Stink Films. OBB was also behind an award-winning “Moisturize Like a Derm” effort that appointed NBA star Kevin Durant as the brand’s “Face of Legs.”

“It's been a campaign that has been working at bringing awareness to the brand, but also to the usage of a body moisturizer, bringing our science to new consumers, particularly men. We've been recruiting more men this year, thanks to this partnership [with the NBA],” Chauvière explained.

The “Dune” partnership is rolling out globally, and the campaign is designed to pair content around the billion-dollar franchise with market-specific dermatologists and experiential activations. CeraVe is growing at a double-digit rate this year and gaining share around the world, and geographic expansion is key to the brand’s future growth, Chauvière said.

“The partnership with ‘Dune’ [is] a way to have a more consistent brand tone of voice and point of view. We have local teams that have a lot of local activations, and the influencer world is a local world. So it's all all about the balance,” the executive said.

The local push builds on CeraVe’s larger creator strategy, which helps the brand reach more than 15 million followers across platforms. The brand this summer united over 100 creators from 22 countries for its first Global CerAwards in Los Angeles. The event included CeraVe Studios, an immersive content creation experience hosted on a Hollywood studio lot, that generated nearly 60 million views of new content, per Chauvière.

“It was a moment of visibility, but it's also a moment to gather all the local influencers together and reunite around this idea of bringing creativity in the beauty world and making science accessible and entertaining at the same time,” the executive said.
